questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
$$ {x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]x+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{3t}\end{aligned}],\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] $$ Write down the expression that gives the solution of the initial value problem above. *Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} & t{e}^{3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{3t}\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}].$*
$x(t)=\,\,$ {{field-1}} $\,\,+{\int }_{0}^{t}\,\,$ $(t-s){e}^{3t}$ $\,\,\text{d}s$
$0$ {{field-2}}
questions.worked_solution:
Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} & t{e}^{3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{3t}\end{aligned}].$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At}\,x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} & t{e}^{3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{3t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{3(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{3(t-s)}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{3(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{3(t-s)}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{3s}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(t-s){e}^{3t} \\ {e}^{3t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}(t-s){e}^{3t} \\ {e}^{3t}\end{aligned}]\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
$$ {x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0\end{aligned}]x+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 5\end{aligned}] $$ Write down the expression that gives the solution of the initial value problem above. *Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0\end{aligned}].$*
$x(t)=\,\,$ $5\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$ $\,\,+{\int }_{0}^{t}\,\,$ {{field-1}} $\,\,\text{d}s$
{{field-2}} $-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s))$
questions.worked_solution:
Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}].$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At}\,x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ 5\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s))\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}5\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ 5\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]+{\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s))\end{aligned}]\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
$$ {x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}]x+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{4t}\end{aligned}],\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] $$ Write down the expression that gives the solution of the initial value problem above. *Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}].$*
$x(t)=\,\,$ $\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)+3\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t)$ $\,\,+{\int }_{0}^{t}\,\,$ ${e}^{4s}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s))$ $\,\,\text{d}s$
{{field-1}} {{field-2}}
questions.worked_solution:
Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}].$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At}\,x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)+3\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t)+3\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{4s}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4s}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ {e}^{4s}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)+3\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t)+3\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]+{\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4s}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ {e}^{4s}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{aligned}]\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
$$ \{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=5x(t)+y(t)+1 \\ {y}^{′}(t)=5y(t),\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] $$ Find the solution to the initial value problem above. *Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{5t} & t{e}^{5t} \\ 0 & {e}^{5t}\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}].$*
$[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{5}\,\,$ {{field-1}}
$0$
questions.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $g(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{5t} & t{e}^{5t} \\ 0 & {e}^{5t}\end{aligned}].
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x(0) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{5t} & t{e}^{5t} \\ 0 & {e}^{5t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{5(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{5(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{5(t-s)}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{5(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{5(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{5(t-s)}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{5(t-s)} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{5(t-s)} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{5}{e}^{5(t-s)} \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}{e}^{5t}-\frac{1}{5} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}{e}^{5t}-\frac{1}{5} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}{e}^{5t}-\frac{1}{5} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{5t}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
$$ \{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=2x(t)+2,\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] $$ Find the solution to the initial value problem above. *Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}].$*
$[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]=\,\,$ {{field-1}}
$\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t)$
questions.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $g(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ 2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ 2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} & t{e}^{3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{3t}\end{aligned}].$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At}\,x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} & t{e}^{3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{3t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{3(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{3(t-s)}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{3(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{3(t-s)}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{3s}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(t-s){e}^{3t} \\ {e}^{3t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}(t-s){e}^{3t} \\ {e}^{3t}\end{aligned}]\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{4s}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4s}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ {e}^{4s}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)+3\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t)+3\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]+{\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4s}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ {e}^{4s}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{aligned}]\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3

x′(t)=[0440]x+[0e4t],x(0)=[13] Write down the expression that gives the solution of the initial value problem above.

Hint: eAt=[cosh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)cosh⁡(4t)], where A=[0440].

x(t)= cosh⁡(4t)+3sinh⁡(4t) +∫0t e4ssinh⁡(4(t−s)) ds
sinh⁡(4t)+3cosh⁡(4t)
sinh⁡(4t)−3cosh⁡(4t)
sinh⁡(4t)+3cosh⁡(4t)
3sinh⁡(4t)+cosh⁡(4t)
3sinh⁡(4t)+3cosh⁡(4t)
e4scosh⁡(4(t−s))
e4scosh⁡(4(t+s))
e4ssinh⁡(4(t−s))
e4ssinh⁡(4(t+s))
e4scosh⁡(4(t−s))
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Given the system x′(t)=Ax(t)+g(t), where A is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution: x(t)=eA(t−t0)x(t0)⏟homogeneous part+∫t0teA(t−s)g(s)ds⏟particular solution, where x(t0) is the initial condition vector.

Let's evaluate each part separately:

$$

$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{5t} & t{e}^{5t} \\ 0 & {e}^{5t}\end{aligned}].
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x(0) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{5t} & t{e}^{5t} \\ 0 & {e}^{5t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$

{x′(t)=2y(t)y′(t)=2x(t)+2,[x(0)y(0)]=[00] Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

Hint: eAt=[cosh⁡(2t)sinh⁡(2t)sinh⁡(2t)cosh⁡(2t)], where A=[0220].

[x(t)y(t)]=
cosh⁡(2t)−1
sinh⁡(t)−1
sinh⁡(t)+1
cosh⁡(2t)−1
cosh⁡(2t)+1
sinh⁡(2t)

Correct
EXPLANATION

Writing our system in matrix form, we get x′(t)=[0220]x(t)+g(t), where x(t)=[x(t)y(t)] and g(t)=[02]. So, the matrix of the system is A=[0220].

Given the system x′(t)=Ax(t)+g(t), where A is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution: x(t)=eA(t−t0)x(t0)⏟homogeneous part+∫t0teA(t−s)g(s)ds⏟particular solution, where x(t0) is the initial condition vector.

Let's evaluate each part separately:

  • First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that eAt=[cosh⁡(2t)sinh⁡(2t)sinh⁡(2t)cosh⁡(2t)]. Since the initial conditions are given at t=t0=0, we have eA(t−t0)=eAtx(0)=[cosh⁡(2t)sinh⁡(2t)sinh⁡(2t)cosh⁡(2t)][00]=[00].

  • Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that eA(t−s)=[cosh⁡(2(t−s))sinh⁡(2(t−s))sinh⁡(2(t−s))cosh⁡(2(t−s))]. So, we have eA(t−s)g(s)=[cosh⁡(2(t−s))sinh⁡(2(t−s))sinh⁡(2(t−s))cosh⁡(2(t−s))][02]=[2sinh⁡(2(t−s))2cosh⁡(2(t−s))]. Thus, we obtain ∫0teA(t−s)g(s)ds=∫0t[2sinh⁡(2(t−s))2cosh⁡(2(t−s))]ds=[−cosh⁡(2(t−s))−sinh⁡(2(t−s))]s=0s=t=[cosh⁡(2t)−1sinh⁡(2t)].

Finally, we get x(t)=[00]+[cosh⁡(2t)−1sinh⁡(2t)]=[cosh⁡(2t)−1sinh⁡(2t)].

question.worked_solution:
Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} & t{e}^{3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{3t}\end{aligned}].$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At}\,x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} & t{e}^{3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{3t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{3(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{3(t-s)}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{3(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{3(t-s)}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{3s}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(t-s){e}^{3t} \\ {e}^{3t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}(t-s){e}^{3t} \\ {e}^{3t}\end{aligned}]\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?
x′(t)=[0440]x+[0e4t],x(0)=[13] Write down the expression that gives the solution of the initial value problem above.

Hint: eAt=[cosh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)cosh⁡(4t)], where A=[0440].

x(t)= cosh⁡(4t)+3sinh⁡(4t) +∫0t e4ssinh⁡(4(t−s)) ds
sinh⁡(4t)+3cosh⁡(4t)
sinh⁡(4t)−3cosh⁡(4t)
sinh⁡(4t)+3cosh⁡(4t)
3sinh⁡(4t)+cosh⁡(4t)
3sinh⁡(4t)+3cosh⁡(4t)
e4scosh⁡(4(t−s))
e4scosh⁡(4(t+s))
e4ssinh⁡(4(t−s))
e4ssinh⁡(4(t+s))
e4scosh⁡(4(t−s))
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Given the system x′(t)=Ax(t)+g(t), where A is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution: x(t)=eA(t−t0)x(t0)⏟homogeneous part+∫t0teA(t−s)g(s)ds⏟particular solution, where x(t0) is the initial condition vector.

Let's evaluate each part separately:

  • First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that eAt=[cosh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)cosh⁡(4t)]. So, eAtx(0)=[cosh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)cosh⁡(4t)][13]=[cosh⁡(4t)+3sinh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)+3cosh⁡(4t)].

  • Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that eA(t−s)=[cosh⁡(4(t−s))sinh⁡(4(t−s))sinh⁡(4(t−s))cosh⁡(4(t−s))]. So, we have eA(t−s)g(s)=[cosh⁡(4(t−s))sinh⁡(4(t−s))sinh⁡(4(t−s))cosh⁡(4(t−s))][0e4s]=[e4ssinh⁡(4(t−s))e4scosh⁡(4(t−s))].

Therefore, we get x(t)=[cosh⁡(4t)+3sinh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)+3cosh⁡(4t)]+∫0t[e4ssinh⁡(4(t−s))e4scosh⁡(4(t−s))]ds.

last_observation.name: Question 3
last_observation.worked_solution:
Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}].$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At}\,x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)+3\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t)+3\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{4s}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4s}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ {e}^{4s}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)+3\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t)+3\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]+{\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4s}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ {e}^{4s}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{aligned}]\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{4s}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4s}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ {e}^{4s}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)+3\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t)+3\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]+{\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4s}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ {e}^{4s}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{aligned}]\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3

x′(t)=[0440]x+[0e4t],x(0)=[13] Write down the expression that gives the solution of the initial value problem above.

Hint: eAt=[cosh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)cosh⁡(4t)], where A=[0440].

x(t)= cosh⁡(4t)+3sinh⁡(4t) +∫0t e4ssinh⁡(4(t−s)) ds
sinh⁡(4t)+3cosh⁡(4t)
sinh⁡(4t)−3cosh⁡(4t)
sinh⁡(4t)+3cosh⁡(4t)
3sinh⁡(4t)+cosh⁡(4t)
3sinh⁡(4t)+3cosh⁡(4t)
e4scosh⁡(4(t−s))
e4scosh⁡(4(t+s))
e4ssinh⁡(4(t−s))
e4ssinh⁡(4(t+s))
e4scosh⁡(4(t−s))
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Given the system x′(t)=Ax(t)+g(t), where A is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution: x(t)=eA(t−t0)x(t0)⏟homogeneous part+∫t0teA(t−s)g(s)ds⏟particular solution, where x(t0) is the initial condition vector.

Let's evaluate each part separately:

  • First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that eAt=[cosh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)cosh⁡(4t)]. So, eAtx(0)=[cosh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)cosh⁡(4t)][13]=[cosh⁡(4t)+3sinh⁡(4t)sinh⁡(4t)+3cosh⁡(4t)].

  • Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that eA(t−s)=[cosh⁡(4(t−s))sinh⁡(4(t−s))sinh⁡(4(t−s))cosh⁡(4(t−s))]. So, we have eA(t−s)g(s)=[cosh⁡(4(t−s))sinh⁡(4(t−s))sinh⁡(4(t−s))cosh⁡(4(t−s))][0e4s]=[e4ssinh⁡(4(t−s))e4scosh⁡(4(t−s))].

$$ {x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}]x+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{4t}\end{aligned}],\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] $$ Write down the expression that gives the solution of the initial value problem above. *Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}].$*
$x(t)=\,\,$ $\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)+3\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t)$ $\,\,+{\int }_{0}^{t}\,\,$ ${e}^{4s}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s))$ $\,\,\text{d}s$

feedback.worked_solution:
Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}].$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At}\,x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)+3\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t)+3\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{4s}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4s}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ {e}^{4s}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)+3\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t)+3\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]+{\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4s}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ {e}^{4s}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{aligned}]\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
$$ \{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=5x(t)+y(t)+1 \\ {y}^{′}(t)=5y(t),\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] $$ Find the solution to the initial value problem above. *Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{5t} & t{e}^{5t} \\ 0 & {e}^{5t}\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}].$*
$[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{5}\,\,$ {{field-1}}
$0$
question.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $g(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{5t} & t{e}^{5t} \\ 0 & {e}^{5t}\end{aligned}].
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x(0) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{5t} & t{e}^{5t} \\ 0 & {e}^{5t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{5(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{5(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{5(t-s)}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{5(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{5(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{5(t-s)}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{5(t-s)} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{5(t-s)} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{5}{e}^{5(t-s)} \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}{e}^{5t}-\frac{1}{5} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}{e}^{5t}-\frac{1}{5} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}{e}^{5t}-\frac{1}{5} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{5t}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t)+g(t),
$$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ 2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ 2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$

Question 5
?
{x′(t)=2y(t)y′(t)=2x(t)+2,[x(0)y(0)]=[00] Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

Hint: eAt=[cosh⁡(2t)sinh⁡(2t)sinh⁡(2t)cosh⁡(2t)], where A=[0220].

[x(t)y(t)]=
cosh⁡(2t)−1
sinh⁡(t)−1
sinh⁡(t)+1
cosh⁡(2t)−1
cosh⁡(2t)+1
sinh⁡(2t)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Writing our system in matrix form, we get x′(t)=[0220]x(t)+g(t), where x(t)=[x(t)y(t)] and g(t)=[02]. So, the matrix of the system is A=[0220].

Given the system x′(t)=Ax(t)+g(t), where A is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution: x(t)=eA(t−t0)x(t0)⏟homogeneous part+∫t0teA(t−s)g(s)ds⏟particular solution, where x(t0) is the initial condition vector.

Let's evaluate each part separately:

  • First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that eAt=[cosh⁡(2t)sinh⁡(2t)sinh⁡(2t)cosh⁡(2t)]. Since the initial conditions are given at t=t0=0, we have eA(t−t0)=eAtx(0)=[cosh⁡(2t)sinh⁡(2t)sinh⁡(2t)cosh⁡(2t)][00]=[00].

  • Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that eA(t−s)=[cosh⁡(2(t−s))sinh⁡(2(t−s))sinh⁡(2(t−s))cosh⁡(2(t−s))]. So, we have eA(t−s)g(s)=[cosh⁡(2(t−s))sinh⁡(2(t−s))sinh⁡(2(t−s))cosh⁡(2(t−s))][02]=[2sinh⁡(2(t−s))2cosh⁡(2(t−s))]. Thus, we obtain ∫0teA(t−s)g(s)ds=∫0t[2sinh⁡(2(t−s))2cosh⁡(2(t−s))]ds=[−cosh⁡(2(t−s))−sinh⁡(2(t−s))]s=0s=t=[cosh⁡(2t)−1sinh⁡(2t)].

Finally, we get x(t)=[00]+[cosh⁡(2t)−1sinh⁡(2t)]=[cosh⁡(2t)−1sinh⁡(2t)].

last_observation.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $g(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ 2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ 2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have eA(t−s)g(s)=[cosh⁡(2(t−s))sinh⁡(2(t−s))sinh⁡(2(t−s))cosh⁡(2(t−s))][02]=[2sinh⁡(2(t−s))2cosh⁡(2(t−s))]. Thus, we obtain ∫0teA(t−s)g(s)ds=∫0t[2sinh⁡(2(t−s))2cosh⁡(2(t−s))]ds=[−cosh⁡(2(t−s))−sinh⁡(2(t−s))]s=0s=t=[cosh⁡(2t)−1sinh⁡(2t)].

Finally, we get x(t)=[00]+[cosh⁡(2t)−1sinh⁡(2t)]=[cosh⁡(2t)−1sinh⁡(2t)].

$$ \{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=2x(t)+2,\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] $$ Find the solution to the initial value problem above. *Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}].$*
$[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]=\,\,$ {{field-1}}
$\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t)$
feedback.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $g(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ 2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ 2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,0,-1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=x{e}^{xy}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡y$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(1,0,-1)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(1,0)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,0) & =1\cdot {e}^{1\cdot 0}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡0 \\  & =1\cdot 1-2\cdot 1 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1,0)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(1,0)}(y-0) \\ z-(-1) & =(-1)y \\ z & =-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,0,-1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ z=-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ Given that the point $P(1,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2y)\operatorname{cos}⁡y$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(1,\frac{\pi }{4}).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(1,\frac{\pi }{4}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot 1\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(1,\frac{\pi }{4}) & ={f}_{x}(1,\frac{\pi }{4})(x-1) \\ z-0 & =1(x-1) \\ z & =x-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=\frac{\pi }{4} \\ z=x-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=\frac{\pi }{4},$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=x-1$ (or $x-z+-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨1,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i-k \\  & =⟨-1,0,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $⟨-1,0,-1⟩$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-⟨-1,0,-1⟩=⟨1,0,1⟩$ is also parallel to it.

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=\sqrt{2}.$ Given that the point $P(\sqrt{2},2,\frac{1}{2})$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=-\frac{2{x}^{2}+y}{{y}^{3}}$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=\sqrt{2}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(\sqrt{2},2,\frac{1}{2})$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(\sqrt{2},2)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(\sqrt{2},2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(\sqrt{2},2) & =-\frac{2(\sqrt{2})^{2}+2}{{2}^{3}} \\  & =-\frac{4+2}{8} \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(\sqrt{2},2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(\sqrt{2},2)}(y-2) \\ z-\frac{1}{2} & =-\frac{3}{4}(y-2) \\ z & =-\frac{3}{4}y+2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(\sqrt{2},2,\frac{1}{2})$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=\sqrt{2} \\ z=-\frac{3}{4}y+2\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=2.$ Given that the point $P(2,\frac{1}{2},1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=x+2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+\frac{1}{y}$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(2,\frac{1}{2}).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(2,\frac{1}{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(2,\frac{1}{2}) & =2+2(2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot \frac{1}{2})+\frac{1}{(1/2)} \\  & =2+4\operatorname{ln}⁡1+2 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(2,\frac{1}{2}) & ={f}_{y}(2,\frac{1}{2})(y-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =4(y-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =4y-2 \\ z & =4y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(2,\frac{1}{2},1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=2 \\ z=4y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=2,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=4y-1$ (or $4y-z-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,4,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,4,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =j+4\,k \\  & =⟨0,1,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $⟨0,1,4⟩.$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Given that the point $P(\frac{\pi }{2},1,0)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}y)$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(\frac{\pi }{2},1).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(\frac{\pi }{2},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(\frac{\pi }{2},1) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 1)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 1) \\  & =2\cdot 1-0 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(\frac{\pi }{2},1) & ={f}_{y}(\frac{\pi }{2},1)(y-1) \\ z-0 & =2(y-1) \\ z & =2y-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(\frac{\pi }{2},1,0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=\frac{\pi }{2} \\ z=2y-2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=\frac{\pi }{2},$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=2y-2$ (or $2y-z-2=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,2,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,2,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =j+2\,k \\  & =⟨0,1,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $⟨0,1,2⟩.$

$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,0,-1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ z=-y-1\end{aligned}

The curve C is the intersection of a surface S, defined by z=f(x,y), with the plane x=1. Given that the point P(1,0,−1) lies on C, and that fy=xexy−2cos⁡y, find the equations of the tangent line to C at P.

b
{x=1z=y−1

{x=1z=−y−1

{x=1z=−2y+1
e
{x=1z=−2y−1
Submit

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(1,\frac{\pi }{4}).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(1,\frac{\pi }{4}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot 1\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(1,\frac{\pi }{4}) & ={f}_{x}(1,\frac{\pi }{4})(x-1) \\ z-0 & =1(x-1) \\ z & =x-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=\frac{\pi }{4} \\ z=x-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=\frac{\pi }{4},$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=x-1$ (or $x-z+-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨1,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i-k \\  & =⟨-1,0,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $⟨-1,0,-1⟩$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-⟨-1,0,-1⟩=⟨1,0,1⟩$ is also parallel to it.

Question 2

The curve C is the intersection of a surface S, defined by z=f(x,y), with the plane y=π4. Given that the point P(1,π4,0) lies on C, and that fx=2sin⁡(2y)cos⁡y, which of the following gives a tangent vector to C at P?

a
⟨1,0,2⟩
b
⟨−1,0,1⟩
c
⟨1,0,2⟩
d
⟨1,0,1⟩
e
⟨−2,0,1⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The curve C is the intersection of the surface with the plane y=π4. Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve C at the point P will be given by the partial derivative fx(1,π4).

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative fx(x,y) at (1,π4):

fx(1,π4)=2sin⁡(2⋅π4)cos⁡π4=2⋅1⋅12=1

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

z−f(1,π4)=fx(1,π4)(x−1)z−0=1(x−1)z=x−1

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve C at P(1,π4,0) can be given as the intersection of two planes: {y=π4z=x−1

Next, notice that:

  • For the plane y=π4, a normal vector to the plane is n1=⟨0,1,0⟩.

  • For the plane z=x−1 (or x−z+−1=0), a normal vector to the plane is n2=⟨1,0,−1⟩.

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

n1×n2=⟨0,1,0⟩×⟨1,0,−1⟩=ijk01010−1=−i−k=⟨−1,0,−1⟩

Finally, since ⟨−1,0,−1⟩ is parallel to the tangent line, then −⟨−1,0,−1⟩=⟨1,0,1⟩ is also parallel to it.

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=\sqrt{2}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(\sqrt{2},2,\frac{1}{2})$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(\sqrt{2},2)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(\sqrt{2},2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(\sqrt{2},2) & =-\frac{2(\sqrt{2})^{2}+2}{{2}^{3}} \\  & =-\frac{4+2}{8} \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(\sqrt{2},2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(\sqrt{2},2)}(y-2) \\ z-\frac{1}{2} & =-\frac{3}{4}(y-2) \\ z & =-\frac{3}{4}y+2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(\sqrt{2},2,\frac{1}{2})$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=\sqrt{2} \\ z=-\frac{3}{4}y+2\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 4
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(2,\frac{1}{2}).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(2,\frac{1}{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(2,\frac{1}{2}) & =2+2(2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot \frac{1}{2})+\frac{1}{(1/2)} \\  & =2+4\operatorname{ln}⁡1+2 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(2,\frac{1}{2}) & ={f}_{y}(2,\frac{1}{2})(y-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =4(y-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =4y-2 \\ z & =4y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(2,\frac{1}{2},1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=2 \\ z=4y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=2,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=4y-1$ (or $4y-z-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,4,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,4,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =j+4\,k \\  & =⟨0,1,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $⟨0,1,4⟩.$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(\frac{\pi }{2},1,0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=\frac{\pi }{2} \\ z=2y-2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=\frac{\pi }{2},$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=2y-2$ (or $2y-z-2=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,2,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,2,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =j+2\,k \\  & =⟨0,1,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $⟨0,1,2⟩.$

question.html:
Question 5
?

The curve C is the intersection of a surface S, defined by z=f(x,y), with the plane x=π2. Given that the point P(π2,1,0) lies on C, and that fy=2sin⁡(xy)−cos⁡(π2y), which of the following gives a tangent vector to C at P?

a
⟨0,1,2⟩
b
⟨0,3,2⟩
c
⟨0,2,−1⟩
d
⟨0,2,3⟩
e
⟨0,1,−3⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The curve C is the intersection of the surface with the plane x=π2. Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve C at the point P will be given by the partial derivative fy(π2,1).

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative fy(x,y) at (π2,1):

fy(π2,1)=2sin⁡(π2⋅1)−cos⁡(π2⋅1)=2⋅1−0=2

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

z−f(π2,1)=fy(π2,1)(y−1)z−0=2(y−1)z=2y−2

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve C at P(π2,1,0) can be given as the intersection of two planes: {x=π2z=2y−2

Next, notice that:

  • For the plane x=π2, a normal vector to the plane is n1=⟨1,0,0⟩.

  • For the plane z=2y−2 (or 2y−z−2=0), a normal vector to the plane is n2=⟨0,2,−1⟩.

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

n1×n2=⟨1,0,0⟩×⟨0,2,−1⟩=ijk10002−1=j+2k=⟨0,1,2⟩

Therefore, a tangent vector to C at P is ⟨0,1,2⟩.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,0,-1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=x{e}^{xy}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡y$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
question.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(1,0,-1)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(1,0)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,0) & =1\cdot {e}^{1\cdot 0}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡0 \\  & =1\cdot 1-2\cdot 1 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1,0)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(1,0)}(y-0) \\ z-(-1) & =(-1)y \\ z & =-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,0,-1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ z=-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ z=-y-1\end{aligned}

e

Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The curve C is the intersection of the surface z=f(x,y) with the plane x=1. Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point P(1,0,−1) will be given by the partial derivative ∂z∂y|(1,0).

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ∂z∂y at (1,0):

fy(1,0)=1⋅e1⋅0−2cos⁡0=1⋅1−2⋅1=−1

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

z−z|(1,0)=∂z∂y|(1,0)(y−0)z−(−1)=(−1)yz=−y−1

Finally, the tangent line to the curve C at P(1,0,−1) can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows: {x=1z=−y−1

solution.reasoning: On x=1, the tangent slope is dz/dy=f_y(1,0)=e^0-2cos(0)=-1. Through P, z+1=-(y-0), so the tangent line is x=1, z=-y-1 (option c). No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its stated key.

feedback.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,0,-1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=x{e}^{xy}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡y$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
feedback.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(1,0,-1)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(1,0)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,0) & =1\cdot {e}^{1\cdot 0}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡0 \\  & =1\cdot 1-2\cdot 1 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1,0)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(1,0)}(y-0) \\ z-(-1) & =(-1)y \\ z & =-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,0,-1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ z=-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ Given that the point $P(1,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2y)\operatorname{cos}⁡y$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
question.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(1,\frac{\pi }{4}).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(1,\frac{\pi }{4}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot 1\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(1,\frac{\pi }{4}) & ={f}_{x}(1,\frac{\pi }{4})(x-1) \\ z-0 & =1(x-1) \\ z & =x-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=\frac{\pi }{4} \\ z=x-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=\frac{\pi }{4},$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=x-1$ (or $x-z+-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨1,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i-k \\  & =⟨-1,0,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $⟨-1,0,-1⟩$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-⟨-1,0,-1⟩=⟨1,0,1⟩$ is also parallel to it.

Question 2

The curve C is the intersection of a surface S, defined by z=f(x,y), with the plane y=π4. Given that the point P(1,π4,0) lies on C, and that fx=2sin⁡(2y)cos⁡y, which of the following gives a tangent vector to C at P?

a
⟨1,0,2⟩
b
⟨−1,0,1⟩
c
⟨1,0,2⟩
d
⟨1,0,1⟩
e
⟨−2,0,1⟩
Submit
Incorrect

The curve C is the intersection of the surface with the plane y=π4. Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve C at the point P will be given by the partial derivative fx(1,π4).

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative fx(x,y) at (1,π4):

fx(1,π4)=2sin⁡(2⋅π4)cos⁡π4=2⋅1⋅12=1

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

z−f(1,π4)=fx(1,π4)(x−1)z−0=1(x−1)z=x−1

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve C at P(1,π4,0) can be given as the intersection of two planes: {y=π4z=x−1

Next, notice that:

  • For the plane y=π4, a normal vector to the plane is n1=⟨0,1,0⟩.

  • For the plane z=x−1 (or x−z+−1=0), a normal vector to the plane is n2=⟨1,0,−1⟩.

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

n1×n2=⟨0,1,0⟩×⟨1,0,−1⟩=ijk01010−1=−i−k=⟨−1,0,−1⟩

Finally, since ⟨−1,0,−1⟩ is parallel to the tangent line, then −⟨−1,0,−1⟩=⟨1,0,1⟩ is also parallel to it.

The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(1,\frac{\pi }{4}).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(1,\frac{\pi }{4}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot 1\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(1,\frac{\pi }{4}) & ={f}_{x}(1,\frac{\pi }{4})(x-1) \\ z-0 & =1(x-1) \\ z & =x-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=\frac{\pi }{4} \\ z=x-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=\frac{\pi }{4},$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=x-1$ (or $x-z+-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨1,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i-k \\  & =⟨-1,0,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $⟨-1,0,-1⟩$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-⟨-1,0,-1⟩=⟨1,0,1⟩$ is also parallel to it.

Question 2
?

The curve C is the intersection of a surface S, defined by z=f(x,y), with the plane y=π4. Given that the point P(1,π4,0) lies on C, and that fx=2sin⁡(2y)cos⁡y, which of the following gives a tangent vector to C at P?

a
⟨1,0,2⟩
b
⟨−1,0,1⟩
c
⟨1,0,2⟩
d
⟨1,0,1⟩
e
⟨−2,0,1⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The curve C is the intersection of the surface with the plane y=π4. Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve C at the point P will be given by the partial derivative fx(1,π4).

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative fx(x,y) at (1,π4):

fx(1,π4)=2sin⁡(2⋅π4)cos⁡π4=2⋅1⋅12=1

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

z−f(1,π4)=fx(1,π4)(x−1)z−0=1(x−1)z=x−1

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve C at P(1,π4,0) can be given as the intersection of two planes: {y=π4z=x−1

Next, notice that:

  • For the plane y=π4, a normal vector to the plane is n1=⟨0,1,0⟩.

  • For the plane z=x−1 (or x−z+−1=0), a normal vector to the plane is n2=⟨1,0,−1⟩.

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

n1×n2=⟨0,1,0⟩×⟨1,0,−1⟩=ijk01010−1=−i−k=⟨−1,0,−1⟩

Finally, since ⟨−1,0,−1⟩ is parallel to the tangent line, then −⟨−1,0,−1⟩=⟨1,0,1⟩ is also parallel to it.

solution.reasoning: Parameterizing C by x gives tangent vector ⟨1,0,f_x⟩. At P, f_x=\sqrt{2}\sin(\pi/2)\cos(\pi/4)=1, so option d is correct. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key.

feedback.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ Given that the point $P(1,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2y)\operatorname{cos}⁡y$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
feedback.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(1,\frac{\pi }{4}).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(1,\frac{\pi }{4}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot 1\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(1,\frac{\pi }{4}) & ={f}_{x}(1,\frac{\pi }{4})(x-1) \\ z-0 & =1(x-1) \\ z & =x-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=\frac{\pi }{4} \\ z=x-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=\frac{\pi }{4},$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=x-1$ (or $x-z+-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨1,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i-k \\  & =⟨-1,0,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $⟨-1,0,-1⟩$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-⟨-1,0,-1⟩=⟨1,0,1⟩$ is also parallel to it.

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=\sqrt{2}.$ Given that the point $P(\sqrt{2},2,\frac{1}{2})$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=-\frac{2{x}^{2}+y}{{y}^{3}}$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
question.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=\sqrt{2}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(\sqrt{2},2,\frac{1}{2})$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(\sqrt{2},2)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(\sqrt{2},2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(\sqrt{2},2) & =-\frac{2(\sqrt{2})^{2}+2}{{2}^{3}} \\  & =-\frac{4+2}{8} \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(\sqrt{2},2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(\sqrt{2},2)}(y-2) \\ z-\frac{1}{2} & =-\frac{3}{4}(y-2) \\ z & =-\frac{3}{4}y+2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(\sqrt{2},2,\frac{1}{2})$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=\sqrt{2} \\ z=-\frac{3}{4}y+2\end{aligned}
$$

b
{x=2z=−14y−2

{x=2z=−32y+1
e
{x=2z=−34y+2

Correct

last_observation.name: Question 3
last_observation.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=\sqrt{2}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(\sqrt{2},2,\frac{1}{2})$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(\sqrt{2},2)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(\sqrt{2},2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(\sqrt{2},2) & =-\frac{2(\sqrt{2})^{2}+2}{{2}^{3}} \\  & =-\frac{4+2}{8} \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(\sqrt{2},2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(\sqrt{2},2)}(y-2) \\ z-\frac{1}{2} & =-\frac{3}{4}(y-2) \\ z & =-\frac{3}{4}y+2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(\sqrt{2},2,\frac{1}{2})$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=\sqrt{2} \\ z=-\frac{3}{4}y+2\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3

The curve C is the intersection of a surface S, defined by z=f(x,y), with the plane x=2. Given that the point P(2,2,12) lies on C, and that fy=−2x2+yy3, find the equations of the tangent line to C at P.

a
{x=2z=32y−1
b
{x=2z=−14y−2
c
{x=2z=12y+2
d
{x=2z=−32y+1
e
{x=2z=−34y+2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The curve C is the intersection of the surface z=f(x,y) with the plane x=2. Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point P(2,2,12) will be given by the partial derivative ∂z∂y|(2,2).

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ∂z∂y at (2,2):

fy(2,2)=−2(2)2+223=−4+28=−34

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

z−z|(2,2)=∂z∂y|(2,2)(y−2)z−12=−34(y−2)z=−34y+2

Finally, the tangent line to the curve C at P(2,2,12) can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows: {x=2z=−34y+2

solution.reasoning: With x fixed at \sqrt{2}, dz/dy=f_y(\sqrt{2},2)=-(2·2+2)/8=-3/4. The tangent line through P satisfies z-1/2=-(3/4)(y-2), giving z=-3y/4+2 and x=\sqrt{2}, option e. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key.

feedback.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=\sqrt{2}.$ Given that the point $P(\sqrt{2},2,\frac{1}{2})$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=-\frac{2{x}^{2}+y}{{y}^{3}}$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
feedback.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=\sqrt{2}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(\sqrt{2},2,\frac{1}{2})$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(\sqrt{2},2)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(\sqrt{2},2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(\sqrt{2},2) & =-\frac{2(\sqrt{2})^{2}+2}{{2}^{3}} \\  & =-\frac{4+2}{8} \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(\sqrt{2},2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(\sqrt{2},2)}(y-2) \\ z-\frac{1}{2} & =-\frac{3}{4}(y-2) \\ z & =-\frac{3}{4}y+2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(\sqrt{2},2,\frac{1}{2})$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=\sqrt{2} \\ z=-\frac{3}{4}y+2\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=2.$ Given that the point $P(2,\frac{1}{2},1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=x+2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+\frac{1}{y}$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
question.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(2,\frac{1}{2}).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(2,\frac{1}{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(2,\frac{1}{2}) & =2+2(2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot \frac{1}{2})+\frac{1}{(1/2)} \\  & =2+4\operatorname{ln}⁡1+2 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(2,\frac{1}{2}) & ={f}_{y}(2,\frac{1}{2})(y-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =4(y-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =4y-2 \\ z & =4y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(2,\frac{1}{2},1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=2 \\ z=4y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=2,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=4y-1$ (or $4y-z-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,4,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,4,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =j+4\,k \\  & =⟨0,1,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $⟨0,1,4⟩.$

Question 4
?

The curve C is the intersection of a surface S, defined by z=f(x,y), with the plane x=2. Given that the point P(2,12,1) lies on C, and that fy=x+2xln⁡(xy)+1y, which of the following gives a tangent vector to C at P?

a
⟨0,1,4⟩
b
⟨0,2,3⟩
c
⟨0,1,3⟩
d
⟨0,1,2⟩
e
⟨0,2,1⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The curve C is the intersection of the surface with the plane x=2. Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve C at the point P will be given by the partial derivative fy(2,12).

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative fy(x,y) at (2,12):

fy(2,12)=2+2(2)ln⁡(2⋅12)+1(1/2)=2+4ln⁡1+2=4

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

z−f(2,12)=fy(2,12)(y−12)z−1=4(y−12)z−1=4y−2z=4y−1

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve C at P(2,12,1) can be given as the intersection of two planes: {x=2z=4y−1

Next, notice that:

  • For the plane x=2, a normal vector to the plane is n1=⟨1,0,0⟩.

  • For the plane z=4y−1 (or 4y−z−1=0), a normal vector to the plane is n2=⟨0,4,−1⟩.

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

n1×n2=⟨1,0,0⟩×⟨0,4,−1⟩=ijk10004−1=j+4k=⟨0,1,4⟩

Therefore, a tangent vector to C at P is ⟨0,1,4⟩.

last_observation.name: Question 4
last_observation.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(2,\frac{1}{2}).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(2,\frac{1}{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(2,\frac{1}{2}) & =2+2(2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot \frac{1}{2})+\frac{1}{(1/2)} \\  & =2+4\operatorname{ln}⁡1+2 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(2,\frac{1}{2}) & ={f}_{y}(2,\frac{1}{2})(y-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =4(y-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =4y-2 \\ z & =4y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(2,\frac{1}{2},1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=2 \\ z=4y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=2,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=4y-1$ (or $4y-z-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,4,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,4,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =j+4\,k \\  & =⟨0,1,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $⟨0,1,4⟩.$

question.html:
Question 4
?

The curve C is the intersection of a surface S, defined by z=f(x,y), with the plane x=2. Given that the point P(2,12,1) lies on C, and that fy=x+2xln⁡(xy)+1y, which of the following gives a tangent vector to C at P?

a
⟨0,1,4⟩
b
⟨0,2,3⟩
c
⟨0,1,3⟩
d
⟨0,1,2⟩
e
⟨0,2,1⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The curve C is the intersection of the surface with the plane x=2. Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve C at the point P will be given by the partial derivative fy(2,12).

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative fy(x,y) at (2,12):

fy(2,12)=2+2(2)ln⁡(2⋅12)+1(1/2)=2+4ln⁡1+2=4

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

z−f(2,12)=fy(2,12)(y−12)z−1=4(y−12)z−1=4y−2z=4y−1

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve C at P(2,12,1) can be given as the intersection of two planes: {x=2z=4y−1

Next, notice that:

  • For the plane x=2, a normal vector to the plane is n1=⟨1,0,0⟩.

  • For the plane z=4y−1 (or 4y−z−1=0), a normal vector to the plane is n2=⟨0,4,−1⟩.

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

n1×n2=⟨1,0,0⟩×⟨0,4,−1⟩=ijk10004−1=j+4k=⟨0,1,4⟩

Therefore, a tangent vector to C at P is ⟨0,1,4⟩.

solution.reasoning: With x=2 fixed, parameterizing by y gives tangent vector ⟨0,1,f_y⟩. At P, f_y=2+4\ln(1)+2=4, so option a is correct. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key.

feedback.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=2.$ Given that the point $P(2,\frac{1}{2},1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=x+2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+\frac{1}{y}$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
feedback.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(2,\frac{1}{2}).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(2,\frac{1}{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(2,\frac{1}{2}) & =2+2(2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot \frac{1}{2})+\frac{1}{(1/2)} \\  & =2+4\operatorname{ln}⁡1+2 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(2,\frac{1}{2}) & ={f}_{y}(2,\frac{1}{2})(y-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =4(y-\frac{1}{2}) \\ z-1 & =4y-2 \\ z & =4y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(2,\frac{1}{2},1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=2 \\ z=4y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=2,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=4y-1$ (or $4y-z-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,4,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,4,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =j+4\,k \\  & =⟨0,1,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $⟨0,1,4⟩.$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Given that the point $P(\frac{\pi }{2},1,0)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}y)$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
question.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(\frac{\pi }{2},1).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(\frac{\pi }{2},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(\frac{\pi }{2},1) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 1)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 1) \\  & =2\cdot 1-0 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(\frac{\pi }{2},1) & ={f}_{y}(\frac{\pi }{2},1)(y-1) \\ z-0 & =2(y-1) \\ z & =2y-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(\frac{\pi }{2},1,0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=\frac{\pi }{2} \\ z=2y-2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=\frac{\pi }{2},$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=2y-2$ (or $2y-z-2=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,2,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,2,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =j+2\,k \\  & =⟨0,1,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $⟨0,1,2⟩.$
