observed_steps.worked_solution:
We see from the graph that as $x$ approaches $6$ from the left, the function $f(x)$ approaches $\infty .$ So, the left-hand limit is

$$
{lim}_{x\to {6}^{-}}f(x)=\infty \,.
$$

Likewise, as $x$ approaches $6$ from the right, the function $f(x)$ again approaches $\infty .$ So, the right-hand limit is

$$
{lim}_{x\to {6}^{+}}f(x)=\infty \,.
$$

Consequently,

$$
{lim}_{x\to 6}f(x)=\infty \,.
$$

question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14250470/assets/d1e5821252dd0634c6033a35247af033bcda8a96fa3733b65be52565a60ea3a6.png)

The figure above shows the graph of $f(x).$ Evaluate ${lim}_{x\to \,\,-2}f(x).$
question.worked_solution:
As $x$ approaches $-2$ from the right, the function value $f(x)$ grows to infinity, and therefore

$$
{lim}_{x\to -{2}^{+}}f(x)=\infty .
$$

However, as $x$ approaches $-2$ from the left, the function value $f(x)$ goes to $-\infty $, and therefore

$$
{lim}_{x\to -{2}^{-}}f(x)=-\infty .
$$

Consequently, 

$$
{lim}_{x\to -2}f(x)=\text{DNE}.
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

The figure above shows the graph of f(x). Evaluate limx→−2f(x).

a
limx→−2f(x)=DNE
b
limx→−2f(x)=∞
c
limx→2f(x)=−∞
d
limx→−2f(x)=−1
e
limx→−2f(x)=−2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

As x approaches −2 from the right, the function value f(x) grows to infinity, and therefore

limx→−2+f(x)=∞.

However, as x approaches −2 from the left, the function value f(x) goes to −∞, and therefore

limx→−2−f(x)=−∞. Consequently, limx→−2f(x)=DNE.

question.html:
Question 1
?

The figure above shows the graph of f(x). Evaluate limx→−2f(x).

a
limx→−2f(x)=DNE
b
limx→−2f(x)=∞
c
limx→2f(x)=−∞
d
limx→−2f(x)=−1
e
limx→−2f(x)=−2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

As x approaches −2 from the right, the function value f(x) grows to infinity, and therefore

limx→−2+f(x)=∞.

However, as x approaches −2 from the left, the function value f(x) goes to −∞, and therefore

limx→−2−f(x)=−∞. Consequently, limx→−2f(x)=DNE.

solution.reasoning: As x approaches -2 from the left, f(x) approaches -∞; from the right, it approaches +∞. The one-sided limits disagree, so the two-sided limit does not exist (option a). No Math Academy answer or grading evidence was supplied.

last_observation.name: Question 3
last_observation.worked_solution:
We see from the graph that as $x$ approaches $-1$ from the left, the function $f(x)$ approaches $-\infty .$ So, the left-hand limit is

$$
{lim}_{x\to (-1)^{-}}f(x)=-\infty \,.
$$

Likewise, as $x$ approaches $-1$ from the right, the function $f(x)$ again approaches $-\infty .$ So, the right-hand limit is

$$
{lim}_{x\to (-1)^{+}}f(x)=-\infty \,.
$$

Consequently,

$$
{lim}_{x\to -1}f(x)=-\infty \,.
$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

The figure above shows the graph of f(x). Evaluate limx→−1f(x).

a
limx→−1f(x)=DNE
b
limx→−1f(x)=−∞
c
limx→−1f(x)=∞
d
limx→−1f(x)=2
e
limx→−1f(x)=−1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We see from the graph that as x approaches −1 from the left, the function f(x) approaches −∞. So, the left-hand limit is

limx→(−1)−f(x)=−∞.

Likewise, as x approaches −1 from the right, the function f(x) again approaches −∞. So, the right-hand limit is

limx→(−1)+f(x)=−∞.

Consequently,

limx→−1f(x)=−∞.

solution.reasoning: Both branches decrease without bound as x approaches -1 from either side. Therefore the limit is -\infty, option b. No Math Academy answer or grading evidence was supplied.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Evaluate $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]$ at $t=1$ given that
$∇f(x,y)=\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+3y}\,i+\frac{3}{{x}^{2}+3y}\,j$
and
$r(t)=t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j.$
questions.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
∇f(x,y)=\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+3y}\,i+\frac{3}{{x}^{2}+3y}\,j.
$$

First, we substitute $x=t$ and $y={t}^{2}$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\frac{2(t)}{(t)^{2}+3({t}^{2})}\,i+\frac{3}{(t)^{2}+3({t}^{2})}\,j \\  & =\frac{2t}{{t}^{2}+3{t}^{2}}\,i+\frac{3}{{t}^{2}+3{t}^{2}}\,j \\  & =\frac{2t}{4{t}^{2}}\,i+\frac{3}{4{t}^{2}}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{2t}\,i+\frac{3}{4{t}^{2}}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,j \\  & =i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\frac{1}{2t}\,i+\frac{3}{4{t}^{2}}\,j)\cdot (i+2t\,j) \\  & =(\frac{1}{2t})\cdot 1+(\frac{3}{4{t}^{2}})\cdot 2t \\  & =\frac{1}{2t}+\frac{3}{2t} \\  & =\frac{4}{2t} \\  & =\frac{2}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=1,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(1))] & =\frac{2}{1}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: If $f(x,y)=2x-x{y}^{2}$ and $r(t)=\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,i+3{t}^{2}\,j,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$
questions.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x-x{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x-x{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =(2-{y}^{2})\,i-2xy\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\operatorname{ln}⁡t$ and $y=3{t}^{2}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =(2-9{t}^{4})\,i-6{t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$

questions.problem: If $f(x,y)=y\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and $r(t)=\pi t\,i+{e}^{t}\,j,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$
questions.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,j \\  & =-y\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\pi t$ and $y={e}^{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,j \\  & =\pi \,i+{e}^{t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\,j)\cdot (\pi \,i+{e}^{t}\,j) \\  & =-\pi {e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t \\  & ={e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: If $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x{y}^{2})$ and $r(t)={t}^{-2}\,i+{e}^{t}\,j,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$
questions.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{x{y}^{2}}\,i+\frac{2xy}{x{y}^{2}}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\,i+\frac{2}{y}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={t}^{-2}$ and $y={e}^{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\frac{1}{{t}^{-2}}\,i+\frac{2}{{e}^{t}}\,j \\  & ={t}^{2}\,i+2{e}^{-t}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{-2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,j \\  & =-2{t}^{-3}\,i+{e}^{t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =({t}^{2}\,i+2{e}^{-t}\,j)\cdot (-2{t}^{-3}\,i+{e}^{t}\,j) \\  & =-2({t}^{2})({t}^{-3})+2{e}^{-t}({e}^{t}) \\  & =2-\frac{2}{t} \\  & =\frac{2(t-1)}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: Evaluate $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]$ at $t=-1$ given that $∇f(x,y)=2x{e}^{{x}^{2}+y}\,i+{e}^{{x}^{2}+y}\,j$ and $r(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t\text{ }i+(t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)\text{ }j.$
questions.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
∇f(x,y)=2x{e}^{{x}^{2}+y}\,i+{e}^{{x}^{2}+y}\,j.
$$

First, we substitute $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ and $y=t+{cos}^{2}⁡t$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{{sin}^{2}⁡t+t+{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,i+{e}^{{sin}^{2}⁡t+t+{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,j \\  & =2{e}^{t+1}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+{e}^{t+1}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+(1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(2{e}^{t+1}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+{e}^{t+1}\,j)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+(1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j) \\  & =2{e}^{t+1}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t+{e}^{t+1}\cdot (1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\  & =2{e}^{t+1}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{e}^{t+1}-2{e}^{t+1}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & ={e}^{t+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=-1,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(-1))] & ={e}^{-1+1}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

In addition, we've been given that ∇f(x,y)=2xx2+3yi+3x2+3yj.

First, we substitute x=t and y=t2 into ∇f(x,y) to find ∇f(r(t)):

If f(x,y)=2x−xy2 and r(t)=ln⁡ti+3t2j, compute ddt[f(r(t))].

a

b

EXPLANATION

The chain rule in vector form states that ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

First, we need to compute ∇f(x,y): ∇f(x,y)=∂∂x(2x−xy2)i+∂∂y(2x−xy2)j=(2−y2)i−2xyj

Next, we substitute x=ln⁡t and y=3t2 into the above to find ∇f(r(t)): ∇f(r(t))=(2−9t4)i−6t2ln⁡tj

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is r′(t)=ddt(ln⁡t)i+ddt(3t2)j=1ti+6tj.

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=((2−9t4)i−6t2ln⁡tj)⋅(1ti+6tj)=(2−9t4)⋅1t+(−6t2ln⁡t)⋅6t=2t−9t3−36t3ln⁡t.

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,j \\  & =\pi \,i+{e}^{t}\,j.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\,j)\cdot (\pi \,i+{e}^{t}\,j) \\  & =-\pi {e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t \\  & ={e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t).\end{aligned}

question.html:
Question 3
?

If f(x,y)=ycos⁡x and r(t)=πti+etj, compute ddt[f(r(t))].

a
 cos⁡πt−etsin⁡πt
b
 πt−etsin⁡πt
c
et(cos⁡πt−πsin⁡πt)
d
 πt+etcos⁡πt
e
 etcos⁡πt−sin⁡πt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule in vector form states that

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

First, we need to compute ∇f(x,y):

∇f(x,y)=∂∂x(ycos⁡x)i+∂∂y(ycos⁡x)j=−ysin⁡xi+cos⁡xj

Next, we substitute x=πt and y=et into the above to find ∇f(r(t)):

∇f(r(t))=−etsin⁡πti+cos⁡πtj

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is

r′(t)=ddt(πt)i+ddt(et)j=πi+etj.

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(−etsin⁡πti+cos⁡πtj)⋅(πi+etj)=−πetsin⁡πt+etcos⁡πt=et(cos⁡πt−πsin⁡πt).

observed_steps.name: Question 4
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{x{y}^{2}}\,i+\frac{2xy}{x{y}^{2}}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\,i+\frac{2}{y}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={t}^{-2}$ and $y={e}^{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\frac{1}{{t}^{-2}}\,i+\frac{2}{{e}^{t}}\,j \\  & ={t}^{2}\,i+2{e}^{-t}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{-2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,j \\  & =-2{t}^{-3}\,i+{e}^{t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =({t}^{2}\,i+2{e}^{-t}\,j)\cdot (-2{t}^{-3}\,i+{e}^{t}\,j) \\  & =-2({t}^{2})({t}^{-3})+2{e}^{-t}({e}^{t}) \\  & =2-\frac{2}{t} \\  & =\frac{2(t-1)}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

If f(x,y)=ln⁡(xy2) and r(t)=t−2i+etj, compute ddt[f(r(t))].

a
2(tet−1)et
b
t(t−2)
c
3(t2+1)t
d
2(t−1)t
e
t2et+2et
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The chain rule in vector form states that

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

First, we need to compute ∇f(x,y):

∇f(x,y)=∂∂xln⁡(xy2)i+∂∂yln⁡(xy2)j=y2xy2i+2xyxy2j=1xi+2yj

Next, we substitute x=t−2 and y=et into the above to find ∇f(r(t)):

∇f(r(t))=1t−2i+2etj=t2i+2e−tj

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is

r′(t)=ddt(t−2)i+ddt(et)j=−2t−3i+etj.

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(t2i+2e−tj)⋅(−2t−3i+etj)=−2(t2)(t−3)+2e−t(et)=2−2t=2(t−1)t.

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
∇f(x,y)=2x{e}^{{x}^{2}+y}\,i+{e}^{{x}^{2}+y}\,j.
$$

First, we substitute $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ and $y=t+{cos}^{2}⁡t$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{{sin}^{2}⁡t+t+{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,i+{e}^{{sin}^{2}⁡t+t+{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,j \\  & =2{e}^{t+1}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+{e}^{t+1}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+(1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(2{e}^{t+1}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+{e}^{t+1}\,j)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+(1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j) \\  & =2{e}^{t+1}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t+{e}^{t+1}\cdot (1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\  & =2{e}^{t+1}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{e}^{t+1}-2{e}^{t+1}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & ={e}^{t+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=-1,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(-1))] & ={e}^{-1+1}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5

Evaluate ddt[f(r(t))] at t=−1 given that ∇f(x,y)=2xex2+yi+ex2+yj and r(t)=sin⁡t i+(t+cos2⁡t) j.

a
2e
b
12
c
2e
d
1
e
e
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule in vector form states that ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

In addition, we've been given that ∇f(x,y)=2xex2+yi+ex2+yj.

First, we substitute x=sin⁡t and y=t+cos2⁡t into ∇f(x,y) to find ∇f(r(t)): ∇f(r(t))=2sin⁡tesin2⁡t+t+cos2⁡ti+esin2⁡t+t+cos2⁡tj=2et+1sin⁡ti+et+1j

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is r′(t)=ddt(sin⁡t)i+ddt(t+cos2⁡t)j=cos⁡ti+(1−2sin⁡tcos⁡t)j.

Applying the chain rule, we get ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(2et+1sin⁡ti+et+1j)⋅(cos⁡ti+(1−2sin⁡tcos⁡t)j)=2et+1sin⁡t⋅cos⁡t+et+1⋅(1−2sin⁡tcos⁡t)=2et+1sin⁡tcos⁡t+et+1−2et+1sin⁡tcos⁡t=et+1.

Finally, evaluating the above at t=−1, we obtain ddt[f(r(−1))]=e−1+1=1.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Evaluate $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]$ at $t=1$ given that
$∇f(x,y)=\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+3y}\,i+\frac{3}{{x}^{2}+3y}\,j$
and
$r(t)=t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j.$
question.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
∇f(x,y)=\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+3y}\,i+\frac{3}{{x}^{2}+3y}\,j.
$$

First, we substitute $x=t$ and $y={t}^{2}$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\frac{2(t)}{(t)^{2}+3({t}^{2})}\,i+\frac{3}{(t)^{2}+3({t}^{2})}\,j \\  & =\frac{2t}{{t}^{2}+3{t}^{2}}\,i+\frac{3}{{t}^{2}+3{t}^{2}}\,j \\  & =\frac{2t}{4{t}^{2}}\,i+\frac{3}{4{t}^{2}}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{2t}\,i+\frac{3}{4{t}^{2}}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,j \\  & =i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\frac{1}{2t}\,i+\frac{3}{4{t}^{2}}\,j)\cdot (i+2t\,j) \\  & =(\frac{1}{2t})\cdot 1+(\frac{3}{4{t}^{2}})\cdot 2t \\  & =\frac{1}{2t}+\frac{3}{2t} \\  & =\frac{4}{2t} \\  & =\frac{2}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=1,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(1))] & =\frac{2}{1}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Evaluate ddt[f(r(t))] at t=1 given that ∇f(x,y)=2xx2+3yi+3x2+3yj and r(t)=ti+t2j.

a
4
b
12
c
1
d
6
e
2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule in vector form states that

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

In addition, we've been given that ∇f(x,y)=2xx2+3yi+3x2+3yj.

First, we substitute x=t and y=t2 into ∇f(x,y) to find ∇f(r(t)):

∇f(r(t))=2(t)(t)2+3(t2)i+3(t)2+3(t2)j=2tt2+3t2i+3t2+3t2j=2t4t2i+34t2j=12ti+34t2j

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is

r′(t)=ddt(t)i+ddt(t2)j=i+2tj.

Applying the chain rule, we get

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(12ti+34t2j)⋅(i+2tj)=(12t)⋅1+(34t2)⋅2t=12t+32t=42t=2t.

Finally, evaluating the above at t=1, we obtain

ddt[f(r(1))]=21=2.

last_observation.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
∇f(x,y)=\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+3y}\,i+\frac{3}{{x}^{2}+3y}\,j.
$$

First, we substitute $x=t$ and $y={t}^{2}$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\frac{2(t)}{(t)^{2}+3({t}^{2})}\,i+\frac{3}{(t)^{2}+3({t}^{2})}\,j \\  & =\frac{2t}{{t}^{2}+3{t}^{2}}\,i+\frac{3}{{t}^{2}+3{t}^{2}}\,j \\  & =\frac{2t}{4{t}^{2}}\,i+\frac{3}{4{t}^{2}}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{2t}\,i+\frac{3}{4{t}^{2}}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,j \\  & =i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\frac{1}{2t}\,i+\frac{3}{4{t}^{2}}\,j)\cdot (i+2t\,j) \\  & =(\frac{1}{2t})\cdot 1+(\frac{3}{4{t}^{2}})\cdot 2t \\  & =\frac{1}{2t}+\frac{3}{2t} \\  & =\frac{4}{2t} \\  & =\frac{2}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=1,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(1))] & =\frac{2}{1}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
Evaluate $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]$ at $t=1$ given that
$∇f(x,y)=\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+3y}\,i+\frac{3}{{x}^{2}+3y}\,j$
and
$r(t)=t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j.$
question.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
∇f(x,y)=\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+3y}\,i+\frac{3}{{x}^{2}+3y}\,j.
$$

First, we substitute $x=t$ and $y={t}^{2}$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\frac{2(t)}{(t)^{2}+3({t}^{2})}\,i+\frac{3}{(t)^{2}+3({t}^{2})}\,j \\  & =\frac{2t}{{t}^{2}+3{t}^{2}}\,i+\frac{3}{{t}^{2}+3{t}^{2}}\,j \\  & =\frac{2t}{4{t}^{2}}\,i+\frac{3}{4{t}^{2}}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{2t}\,i+\frac{3}{4{t}^{2}}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,j \\  & =i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\frac{1}{2t}\,i+\frac{3}{4{t}^{2}}\,j)\cdot (i+2t\,j) \\  & =(\frac{1}{2t})\cdot 1+(\frac{3}{4{t}^{2}})\cdot 2t \\  & =\frac{1}{2t}+\frac{3}{2t} \\  & =\frac{4}{2t} \\  & =\frac{2}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=1,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(1))] & =\frac{2}{1}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: If $f(x,y)=2x-x{y}^{2}$ and $r(t)=\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,i+3{t}^{2}\,j,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$
question.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x-x{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x-x{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =(2-{y}^{2})\,i-2xy\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\operatorname{ln}⁡t$ and $y=3{t}^{2}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =(2-9{t}^{4})\,i-6{t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2})\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{t}\,i+6t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =((2-9{t}^{4})\,i-6{t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,j)\cdot (\frac{1}{t}\,i+6t\,j) \\  & =(2-9{t}^{4})\cdot \frac{1}{t}+(-6{t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)\cdot 6t \\  & =\frac{2}{t}-9{t}^{3}-36{t}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

If f(x,y)=2x−xy2 and r(t)=ln⁡ti+3t2j, compute ddt[f(r(t))].

a
2t−9t3−36t3ln⁡t
b
2+9t3+6t3ln⁡t
c
2t−3t−3tln⁡t
d
2t−3t2+36t3
e
2t−9t2−12t2ln⁡t
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The chain rule in vector form states that ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

First, we need to compute ∇f(x,y): ∇f(x,y)=∂∂x(2x−xy2)i+∂∂y(2x−xy2)j=(2−y2)i−2xyj

Next, we substitute x=ln⁡t and y=3t2 into the above to find ∇f(r(t)): ∇f(r(t))=(2−9t4)i−6t2ln⁡tj

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is r′(t)=ddt(ln⁡t)i+ddt(3t2)j=1ti+6tj.

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=((2−9t4)i−6t2ln⁡tj)⋅(1ti+6tj)=(2−9t4)⋅1t+(−6t2ln⁡t)⋅6t=2t−9t3−36t3ln⁡t.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x-x{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x-x{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =(2-{y}^{2})\,i-2xy\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\operatorname{ln}⁡t$ and $y=3{t}^{2}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =(2-9{t}^{4})\,i-6{t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2})\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{t}\,i+6t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =((2-9{t}^{4})\,i-6{t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,j)\cdot (\frac{1}{t}\,i+6t\,j) \\  & =(2-9{t}^{4})\cdot \frac{1}{t}+(-6{t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)\cdot 6t \\  & =\frac{2}{t}-9{t}^{3}-36{t}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

If f(x,y)=2x−xy2 and r(t)=ln⁡ti+3t2j, compute ddt[f(r(t))].

a
2t−9t3−36t3ln⁡t
b
2+9t3+6t3ln⁡t
c
2t−3t−3tln⁡t
d
2t−3t2+36t3
e
2t−9t2−12t2ln⁡t
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The chain rule in vector form states that ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

First, we need to compute ∇f(x,y): ∇f(x,y)=∂∂x(2x−xy2)i+∂∂y(2x−xy2)j=(2−y2)i−2xyj

Next, we substitute x=ln⁡t and y=3t2 into the above to find ∇f(r(t)): ∇f(r(t))=(2−9t4)i−6t2ln⁡tj

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is r′(t)=ddt(ln⁡t)i+ddt(3t2)j=1ti+6tj.

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=((2−9t4)i−6t2ln⁡tj)⋅(1ti+6tj)=(2−9t4)⋅1t+(−6t2ln⁡t)⋅6t=2t−9t3−36t3ln⁡t.

solution.reasoning: Substitution gives f(r(t))=2\ln t-9t^4\ln t for t>0. Differentiating with the product rule yields 2/t-36t^3\ln t-9t^3, matching option a. No Math Academy answer or grading evidence was supplied.

\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,j \\  & =-y\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,j\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,j \\  & =\pi \,i+{e}^{t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\,j)\cdot (\pi \,i+{e}^{t}\,j) \\  & =-\pi {e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t \\  & ={e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

If f(x,y)=ycos⁡x and r(t)=πti+etj, compute ddt[f(r(t))].

a
 cos⁡πt−etsin⁡πt
b
 πt−etsin⁡πt
c
et(cos⁡πt−πsin⁡πt)
d
 πt+etcos⁡πt
e
 etcos⁡πt−sin⁡πt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule in vector form states that

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

First, we need to compute ∇f(x,y):

∇f(x,y)=∂∂x(ycos⁡x)i+∂∂y(ycos⁡x)j=−ysin⁡xi+cos⁡xj

Next, we substitute x=πt and y=et into the above to find ∇f(r(t)):

∇f(r(t))=−etsin⁡πti+cos⁡πtj

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is

r′(t)=ddt(πt)i+ddt(et)j=πi+etj.

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(−etsin⁡πti+cos⁡πtj)⋅(πi+etj)=−πetsin⁡πt+etcos⁡πt=et(cos⁡πt−πsin⁡πt).

question.html:
Question 3
?

If f(x,y)=ycos⁡x and r(t)=πti+etj, compute ddt[f(r(t))].

a
 cos⁡πt−etsin⁡πt
b
 πt−etsin⁡πt
c
et(cos⁡πt−πsin⁡πt)
d
 πt+etcos⁡πt
e
 etcos⁡πt−sin⁡πt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule in vector form states that

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

First, we need to compute ∇f(x,y):

∇f(x,y)=∂∂x(ycos⁡x)i+∂∂y(ycos⁡x)j=−ysin⁡xi+cos⁡xj

Next, we substitute x=πt and y=et into the above to find ∇f(r(t)):

∇f(r(t))=−etsin⁡πti+cos⁡πtj

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is

r′(t)=ddt(πt)i+ddt(et)j=πi+etj.

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(−etsin⁡πti+cos⁡πtj)⋅(πi+etj)=−πetsin⁡πt+etcos⁡πt=et(cos⁡πt−πsin⁡πt).

solution.reasoning: Substitution gives f(r(t))=e^t\cos(\pi t). The product and chain rules give e^t\cos(\pi t)-\pi e^t\sin(\pi t), matching option c. No Math Academy answer or grading evidence was supplied.

question.problem: If $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x{y}^{2})$ and $r(t)={t}^{-2}\,i+{e}^{t}\,j,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$
question.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{x{y}^{2}}\,i+\frac{2xy}{x{y}^{2}}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\,i+\frac{2}{y}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={t}^{-2}$ and $y={e}^{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\frac{1}{{t}^{-2}}\,i+\frac{2}{{e}^{t}}\,j \\  & ={t}^{2}\,i+2{e}^{-t}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{-2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,j \\  & =-2{t}^{-3}\,i+{e}^{t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =({t}^{2}\,i+2{e}^{-t}\,j)\cdot (-2{t}^{-3}\,i+{e}^{t}\,j) \\  & =-2({t}^{2})({t}^{-3})+2{e}^{-t}({e}^{t}) \\  & =2-\frac{2}{t} \\  & =\frac{2(t-1)}{t}.\end{aligned}

Question 4
?

If f(x,y)=ln⁡(xy2) and r(t)=t−2i+etj, compute ddt[f(r(t))].

a
2(tet−1)et
b
t(t−2)
c
3(t2+1)t
d
2(t−1)t
e
t2et+2et
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The chain rule in vector form states that

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

First, we need to compute ∇f(x,y):

∇f(x,y)=∂∂xln⁡(xy2)i+∂∂yln⁡(xy2)j=y2xy2i+2xyxy2j=1xi+2yj

Next, we substitute x=t−2 and y=et into the above to find ∇f(r(t)):

∇f(r(t))=1t−2i+2etj=t2i+2e−tj

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is

r′(t)=ddt(t−2)i+ddt(et)j=−2t−3i+etj.

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(t2i+2e−tj)⋅(−2t−3i+etj)=−2(t2)(t−3)+2e−t(et)=2−2t=2(t−1)t.

last_observation.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{x{y}^{2}}\,i+\frac{2xy}{x{y}^{2}}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\,i+\frac{2}{y}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={t}^{-2}$ and $y={e}^{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\frac{1}{{t}^{-2}}\,i+\frac{2}{{e}^{t}}\,j \\  & ={t}^{2}\,i+2{e}^{-t}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{-2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,j \\  & =-2{t}^{-3}\,i+{e}^{t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =({t}^{2}\,i+2{e}^{-t}\,j)\cdot (-2{t}^{-3}\,i+{e}^{t}\,j) \\  & =-2({t}^{2})({t}^{-3})+2{e}^{-t}({e}^{t}) \\  & =2-\frac{2}{t} \\  & =\frac{2(t-1)}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

If f(x,y)=ln⁡(xy2) and r(t)=t−2i+etj, compute ddt[f(r(t))].

a
2(tet−1)et
b
t(t−2)
c
3(t2+1)t
d
2(t−1)t
e

Submit

EXPLANATION

The chain rule in vector form states that

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

First, we need to compute ∇f(x,y):

∇f(x,y)=∂∂xln⁡(xy2)i+∂∂yln⁡(xy2)j=y2xy2i+2xyxy2j=1xi+2yj

Next, we substitute x=t−2 and y=et into the above to find ∇f(r(t)):

∇f(r(t))=1t−2i+2etj=t2i+2e−tj

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is

r′(t)=ddt(t−2)i+ddt(et)j=−2t−3i+etj.

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(t2i+2e−tj)⋅(−2t−3i+etj)=−2(t2)(t−3)+2e−t(et)=2−2t=2(t−1)t.

feedback.problem: If $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x{y}^{2})$ and $r(t)={t}^{-2}\,i+{e}^{t}\,j,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$
feedback.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{x{y}^{2}}\,i+\frac{2xy}{x{y}^{2}}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\,i+\frac{2}{y}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={t}^{-2}$ and $y={e}^{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\frac{1}{{t}^{-2}}\,i+\frac{2}{{e}^{t}}\,j \\  & ={t}^{2}\,i+2{e}^{-t}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{-2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,j \\  & =-2{t}^{-3}\,i+{e}^{t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =({t}^{2}\,i+2{e}^{-t}\,j)\cdot (-2{t}^{-3}\,i+{e}^{t}\,j) \\  & =-2({t}^{2})({t}^{-3})+2{e}^{-t}({e}^{t}) \\  & =2-\frac{2}{t} \\  & =\frac{2(t-1)}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: Evaluate $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]$ at $t=-1$ given that $∇f(x,y)=2x{e}^{{x}^{2}+y}\,i+{e}^{{x}^{2}+y}\,j$ and $r(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t\text{ }i+(t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)\text{ }j.$
question.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
∇f(x,y)=2x{e}^{{x}^{2}+y}\,i+{e}^{{x}^{2}+y}\,j.
$$

First, we substitute $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ and $y=t+{cos}^{2}⁡t$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{{sin}^{2}⁡t+t+{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,i+{e}^{{sin}^{2}⁡t+t+{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,j \\  & =2{e}^{t+1}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+{e}^{t+1}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+(1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(2{e}^{t+1}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+{e}^{t+1}\,j)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+(1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j) \\  & =2{e}^{t+1}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t+{e}^{t+1}\cdot (1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\  & =2{e}^{t+1}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{e}^{t+1}-2{e}^{t+1}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & ={e}^{t+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=-1,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(-1))] & ={e}^{-1+1}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
∇f(x,y)=2x{e}^{{x}^{2}+y}\,i+{e}^{{x}^{2}+y}\,j.
$$

First, we substitute $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ and $y=t+{cos}^{2}⁡t$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{{sin}^{2}⁡t+t+{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,i+{e}^{{sin}^{2}⁡t+t+{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,j \\  & =2{e}^{t+1}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+{e}^{t+1}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+(1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(2{e}^{t+1}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+{e}^{t+1}\,j)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+(1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j) \\  & =2{e}^{t+1}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t+{e}^{t+1}\cdot (1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\  & =2{e}^{t+1}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{e}^{t+1}-2{e}^{t+1}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & ={e}^{t+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=-1,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(-1))] & ={e}^{-1+1}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate ddt[f(r(t))] at t=−1 given that ∇f(x,y)=2xex2+yi+ex2+yj and r(t)=sin⁡t i+(t+cos2⁡t) j.

EXPLANATION

The chain rule in vector form states that ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

In addition, we've been given that ∇f(x,y)=2xex2+yi+ex2+yj.

First, we substitute x=sin⁡t and y=t+cos2⁡t into ∇f(x,y) to find ∇f(r(t)): ∇f(r(t))=2sin⁡tesin2⁡t+t+cos2⁡ti+esin2⁡t+t+cos2⁡tj=2et+1sin⁡ti+et+1j

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is r′(t)=ddt(sin⁡t)i+ddt(t+cos2⁡t)j=cos⁡ti+(1−2sin⁡tcos⁡t)j.

Applying the chain rule, we get ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(2et+1sin⁡ti+et+1j)⋅(cos⁡ti+(1−2sin⁡tcos⁡t)j)=2et+1sin⁡t⋅cos⁡t+et+1⋅(1−2sin⁡tcos⁡t)=2et+1sin⁡tcos⁡t+et+1−2et+1sin⁡tcos⁡t=et+1.

Finally, evaluating the above at t=−1, we obtain ddt[f(r(−1))]=e−1+1=1.

solution.reasoning: The chain rule gives ∇f(r(t))·r'(t). Along the curve, x²+y=sin²t+t+cos²t=t+1 and r'(t)=(cos t,1−2sin t cos t). Thus the derivative is e^{t+1}[2sin t cos t+1−2sin t cos t]=e^{t+1}, which equals 1 at t=−1. This matches option d; no Math Academy answer or grading evidence was supplied.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14249971/assets/861e191e0f0b0d993e2d16f29da17ec9e258d657f6bdfc471e5fa9cf21a67b21.png)

The function $f(x)$ is defined and differentiable on $[-3,2].$ The graph of ${f}^{′}(x),$ the derivative of $f(x),$ is shown above. Find the maximum value of the function $f(x)$ on the interval $[-3,2]$ given that $f(2)=4.$
questions.worked_solution:
According to the candidates test, the maximum value of $f(x)$ on $[-3,2]$ must occur at a critical point or an endpoint of the interval. 

**Step 1**: Find the critical points:

We see that ${f}^{′}(x)$ is defined everywhere on $x\in (-3,2),$ and ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ at $x=-1$ Therefore, the candidates are $x=-3,-1,2.$

**Step 2**: Compute the value of $f$ for each candidate using the fundamental theorem of calculus:

The function is made up of $1$ trapezoid and $1$ triangle. Let's add the areas bounded by these shapes to our diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14249971/assets/b7f6e2f43ae474ec3194b2395144e8ea7dc9964da65bd018af08bb24b873bdd4.png)

Using the given information and the fundamental theorem of calculus, we have the following:

$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14250552/assets/2c1790cb306a749737594f994f6893d0146d5f2ed2458dc9e50ff9f4278475d7.png)

The graph above shows $y=k({3}^{x}).$ What is the value of the constant $k?$
questions.worked_solution:
To plot the graph of $y=k({3}^{x})$ we take the graph of $y={3}^{x}$ and stretch it vertically by a scale factor of  $k.$ Under the action of this transformation, the $y$-intercept is mapped from $(0,1)$ to $(0,k)$

Comparing the point $(0,1.5)$ on the graph to $(0,k),$ we see that we must have $k=1.5.$

questions.problem:
| $f$ | $Y=-2$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=2$ | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | $X=0$ | $0.16$ | $0.09$ | $0.05$ | | $X=1$ | $0.44$ | $0.21$ | $0.05$ | The joint probability distribution $f(x,y)$ of the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given above, while the marginal mass functions for these variables are shown below.
$x$ $0$ $1$
${f}_{X}(x)$ $0.3$ $0.7$

$y$ $-2$ $0$ $2$
${f}_{Y}(y)$ $0.6$ $0.3$ $0.1$

Which of the following statements are true? I. $P(X=0,Y=0)=P(X=0)\cdot P(Y=0)$ II. $P(X=x,Y=y)=P(X=x)\cdot P(Y=y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y$ III. $X$ and $Y$ are independent
questions.worked_solution:
Two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with a joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability mass functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. From the table, we obtain that $P(X=0,Y=0)=f(0,0)=0.09.$ On the other hand, 

$$
P(X=0)\cdot P(Y=0)={f}_{X}(0)\cdot {f}_{Y}(0)=0.3\cdot 0.3=0.09.\,✓
$$

- Statement II is false. Checking some possible products, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,-2) & =0.16\ne 0.3\cdot 0.6={f}_{X}(0)\cdot {f}_{Y}(-2) & \times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $P(X=x,Y=y)\ne P(X=x)\cdot P(Y=y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y.$

- Statement III is false. Since statement II is false, our random variables $X$ and $Y$ are *not* independent.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $P(X=3,Y=2)=P(X=3)\cdot P(Y=2)$

II. $P(X=x,Y=y)=P(X=x)\cdot P(Y=y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y$

III. $X$ and $Y$ are independent
questions.worked_solution:
Two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with a joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 
for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability mass functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

Computing the marginal probability mass functions for  $X$ and $Y,$ we obtain the following:

| $f$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=4$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=1$ | $0.7$ | $0.1$ | $0.8$ |
| $X=3$ | $0.1$ | $0.1$ | $0.2$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.8$ | $0.2$ | $1$ |

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statements I and II are false. From the table, we obtain that $P(X=3,Y=2)=f(3,2)=0.1.$ However, 

$$
P(X=3)\cdot P(Y=2)={f}_{X}(3)\cdot {f}_{Y}(2)=0.2\cdot 0.8=0.16.\,\times 
$$

Therefore, 

$$
P(X=3,Y=2)\ne P(X=3)\cdot P(Y=2),
$$

and $P(X=x,Y=y)\ne P(X=x)\cdot P(Y=y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y.$

- Statement III is false. Since statement II is false, our random variables $X$ and $Y$ are *not* independent.

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of those listed."

questions.worked_solution:
Two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with a joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability mass functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

Therefore, since our random variables are independent, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2,5) & ={f}_{X}(2)\cdot {f}_{Y}(5) \\ P(X=2,Y=5) & =P(X=2)\cdot P(Y=5) \\ 0.09 & =0.45\cdot P(Y=5) \\ P(Y=5) & =\frac{0.09}{0.45} \\  & =0.2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 15
questions.problem:
The partially complete joint probability distribution $f(x,y)$ of the independent discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ is below. 

| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=5$ | $0.12$ | $∗$ | $?$ |
| $X=7$ | $0.24$ | $∗$ | $∗$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.36$ | $0.64$ | $1$ |

What is the value of $P(X=5)?$
questions.worked_solution:
Two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with a joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability mass functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

Therefore, since our random variables are independent, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(5,0) & ={f}_{X}(5)\cdot {f}_{Y}(0) \\ P(X=5,Y=0) & =P(X=5)\cdot P(Y=0) \\ 0.12 & =P(X=5)\cdot 0.36 \\ P(X=5) & =\frac{0.12}{0.36} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Determining Whether Two Random Variables are Independent
canonical_examples.problem:
| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ | | --- | --- | --- | | $X=0$ | $0.24$ | $0.06$ | | $X=1$ | $0.56$ | $0.14$ | The joint probability distribution $f(x,y)$ of the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given above, while the marginal mass functions for these variables are shown below.
$x$ $0$ $1$
$f_X(x)$ $0.3$ $0.7$

$y$ $0$ $1$
$f_Y(y)$ $0.8$ $0.2$

Which of the following statements are true? I. $P({X = 0}, {Y = 0}) = P(X=0) \cdot P(Y=0)$ II. $P({X = x}, {Y = y}) = P(X=x) \cdot P(Y=y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y$ III. $X$ and $Y$ are independent
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with a joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x, y) = f_X(x) \cdot f_Y (y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where $f_X(x)$ and $f_Y (y)$ are the marginal probability mass functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. From the table, we obtain that $P({X = 0}, {Y = 0}) = f(0,0) = 0.24.$ On the other hand, 

$$
P(X=0) \cdot P(Y=0) = f_X(0) \cdot f_Y(0) = 0.3 \cdot 0.8 = 0.24. \quad {\color{green}\checkmark}
$$

- Statement II is true. Checking all other possible products, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,0) & =0.56=0.7\cdot 0.8={f}_{X}(1)\cdot {f}_{Y}(0) & ✓ \\ f(0,1) & =0.06=0.3\cdot 0.2={f}_{X}(0)\cdot {f}_{Y}(1) & ✓ \\ f(1,1) & =0.14=0.7\cdot 0.2={f}_{X}(1)\cdot {f}_{Y}(1) & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, $P({X = x}, {Y = y}) = P(X=x) \cdot P(Y=y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y.$

- Statement III is true. Since statement II is true, our random variables $X$ and $Y$ must be independent.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

$$

$$

- Statement II is true. Checking all other possible products, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,1) & =0.12=0.4\cdot 0.3={f}_{X}(0)\cdot {f}_{Y}(1) & ✓ \\ f(1,0) & =0.42=0.6\cdot 0.7={f}_{X}(1)\cdot {f}_{Y}(0) & ✓ \\ f(1,1) & =0.18=0.6\cdot 0.3={f}_{X}(1)\cdot {f}_{Y}(1) & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, $P({X = x}, {Y = y}) = P(X=x) \cdot P(Y=y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y.$

- Statement III is true. Since statement II is true, our random variables $X$ and $Y$ must be independent.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be discrete random variables with supports $S_X$ and $S_Y,$ respectively. We say that $X$ and $Y$ are **independent** if, for all $x\in S_X$ and $y\in S_Y,$ we have 

$$
P(X=x, Y=y)=P(X=x)\cdot P(Y=y).
$$

Moreover, if $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability mass function $f(x,y),$ and $f_X(x)$ and $f_Y(y)$ are the marginal mass functions of $X$ and $Y,$ respectively, then

$$
f(x, y) = f_X(x)\cdot f_Y (y)
$$

 

for all $x\in S_X$ and $y\in S_Y.$

If the random variables are not independent, they are **dependent**.

$x$ $0$ $1$

$y$ $-2$ $0$ $2$
${f}_{Y}(y)$ $0.6$ $0.3$ $0.1$

Which of the following statements are true? I. $P(X=0,Y=0)=P(X=0)\cdot P(Y=0)$ II. $P(X=x,Y=y)=P(X=x)\cdot P(Y=y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y$ III. $X$ and $Y$ are independent
question.worked_solution:
Two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with a joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability mass functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. From the table, we obtain that $P(X=0,Y=0)=f(0,0)=0.09.$ On the other hand, 

$$
P(X=0)\cdot P(Y=0)={f}_{X}(0)\cdot {f}_{Y}(0)=0.3\cdot 0.3=0.09.\,✓
$$

- Statement II is false. Checking some possible products, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,-2) & =0.16\ne 0.3\cdot 0.6={f}_{X}(0)\cdot {f}_{Y}(-2) & \times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $P(X=x,Y=y)\ne P(X=x)\cdot P(Y=y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y.$

- Statement III is false. Since statement II is false, our random variables $X$ and $Y$ are *not* independent.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

$$

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Calculating Joint Probabilities
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with a joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability mass functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

Therefore, since our random variables are independent, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(5,0) & ={f}_{X}(5)\cdot {f}_{Y}(0) \\ P(X=5,Y=0) & =P(X=5)\cdot P(Y=0) \\ 0.12 & =P(X=5)\cdot 0.36 \\ P(X=5) & =\frac{0.12}{0.36} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus I and II are true, and the factorization establishes independence, so III is true. No MA answer or grade for this question is captured; the supplied worked solution addresses a different example.

feedback.problem:
| $f$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=4$ | | --- | --- | --- | | $X=0$ | $0.15$ | $0.45$ | | $X=1$ | $0.1$ | $0.3$ | The joint probability distribution $f(x,y)$ of the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given above, while the marginal mass functions for these variables are shown below.
$x$ $0$ $1$
${f}_{X}(x)$ $0.6$ $0.4$

$y$ $2$ $4$
${f}_{Y}(y)$ $0.25$ $0.75$

Which of the following statements are true? I. $P(X=0,Y=2)=P(X=0)\cdot P(Y=2)$ II. $P(X=x,Y=y)=P(X=x)\cdot P(Y=y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y$ III. $X$ and $Y$ are independent
feedback.worked_solution:
Two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with a joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability mass functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. From the table, we obtain that $P(X=0,Y=2)=f(0,2)=0.15.$ On the other hand, 

$$
P(X=0)\cdot P(Y=2)={f}_{X}(0)\cdot {f}_{Y}(2)=0.6\cdot 0.25=0.15.\,✓
$$

- Statement II is true. Checking all other possible products, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,4) & =0.45=0.6\cdot 0.75={f}_{X}(0)\cdot {f}_{Y}(4) & ✓ \\ f(1,2) & =0.1=0.4\cdot 0.25={f}_{X}(1)\cdot {f}_{Y}(2) & ✓ \\ f(1,4) & =0.3=0.4\cdot 0.75={f}_{X}(1)\cdot {f}_{Y}(4) & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, $P(X=x,Y=y)=P(X=x)\cdot P(Y=y)$ for all possible $x$ and $y.$

- Statement III is true. Since statement II is true, our random variables $X$ and $Y$ must be independent.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

$$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability mass functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statements I and II are false. From the table, we obtain that $P(X=0,Y=1)=f(0,1)=0.32.$ However, 

$$
P(X=0)\cdot P(Y=1)={f}_{X}(0)\cdot {f}_{Y}(1)=0.7\cdot 0.6=0.42.\,\times

$$
P(X=0,Y=1)\ne P(X=0)\cdot P(Y=1),

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true."

question.name: Question 15
question.problem:
The partially complete joint probability distribution $f(x,y)$ of the independent discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ is below. 

| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=5$ | $0.12$ | $∗$ | $?$ |
| $X=7$ | $0.24$ | $∗$ | $∗$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.36$ | $0.64$ | $1$ |

What is the value of $P(X=5)?$
question.worked_solution:
Two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with a joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability mass functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

Therefore, since our random variables are independent, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(5,0) & ={f}_{X}(5)\cdot {f}_{Y}(0) \\ P(X=5,Y=0) & =P(X=5)\cdot P(Y=0) \\ 0.12 & =P(X=5)\cdot 0.36 \\ P(X=5) & =\frac{0.12}{0.36} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 15
?

The partially complete joint probability distribution f(x,y) of the independent discrete random variables X and Y is below.

f Y=0 Y=1 fX
X=5 0.12 ∗ ?
X=7 0.24 ∗ ∗
fY 0.36 0.64 1

What is the value of P(X=5)?

a
14
b
12
c
13
d
23
e
16
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Two discrete random variables X and Y with a joint probability mass function f(x,y) are independent if and only if

f(x,y)=fX(x)⋅fY(y)

for all possible values x and y, where fX(x) and fY(y) are the marginal probability mass functions for X and Y, respectively.

Therefore, since our random variables are independent, we have

f(5,0)=fX(5)⋅fY(0)P(X=5,Y=0)=P(X=5)⋅P(Y=0)0.12=P(X=5)⋅0.36P(X=5)=0.120.36=13.
question.knowledge_point: Calculating Joint Probabilities

last_observation.worked_solution:
Two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with a joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability mass functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

Therefore, since our random variables are independent, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(5,0) & ={f}_{X}(5)\cdot {f}_{Y}(0) \\ P(X=5,Y=0) & =P(X=5)\cdot P(Y=0) \\ 0.12 & =P(X=5)\cdot 0.36 \\ P(X=5) & =\frac{0.12}{0.36} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.html:
Question 15
?

The partially complete joint probability distribution f(x,y) of the independent discrete random variables X and Y is below.

f Y=0 Y=1 fX
X=5 0.12 ∗ ?
X=7 0.24 ∗ ∗
fY 0.36 0.64 1

What is the value of P(X=5)?

a
14
b
12
c
13
d
23
e
16
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Two discrete random variables X and Y with a joint probability mass function f(x,y) are independent if and only if

f(x,y)=fX(x)⋅fY(y)

for all possible values x and y, where fX(x) and fY(y) are the marginal probability mass functions for X and Y, respectively.

Therefore, since our random variables are independent, we have

f(5,0)=fX(5)⋅fY(0)P(X=5,Y=0)=P(X=5)⋅P(Y=0)0.12=P(X=5)⋅0.36P(X=5)=0.120.36=13.

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Calculate ${lim}_{x\to (-4)}{log}_{2}⁡(x+4).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's sketch the graph of $y={log}_{2}⁡(x+4).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14250624/assets/57f95a683f7f9c06287bfed1bc459df33dbcdfcdf253d6878e0c77de60d906e0.png)

The function is not defined for $x\le -4.$ Therefore,

$$
{lim}_{x\to -{4}^{-}}{log}_{2}⁡(x+4)=\text{DNE}.
$$

However, the function is defined for $x>-4.$ Moreover,

$$
{lim}_{x\to -{4}^{+}}{log}_{2}⁡(x+4)=-\infty .
$$

Since the left and right-sided limits are not equal, we have

$$
{lim}_{x\to -4}{log}_{2}⁡(x+4)=\text{DNE}.
$$

Let's sketch the graph of $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14250624/assets/52817b9c0ede04e8e920de8a52ebe025916f314cc937097c7fb91ea612e18f1b.png)

The function is not defined for $x\le -1.$ Therefore,

$$
{lim}_{x\to -{1}^{-}}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)=\text{DNE}.
$$

However, the function is defined for $x>-1.$ Moreover,

$$
{lim}_{x\to -{1}^{+}}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)=-\infty .
$$

Since the left and right-sided limits are not equal, we have

$$
{lim}_{x\to -1}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)=\text{DNE}.
$$

Let's sketch the graph of y=log2⁡(x+4).

The function is not defined for x≤−4. Therefore,

limx→−4−log2⁡(x+4)=DNE.

However, the function is defined for x>−4. Moreover,

limx→−4+log2⁡(x+4)=−∞.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Suppose that a $3\times 3$ matrix $C$ is reduced to row echelon form using the following elementary row operations, applied in the order in which they appear:

$$
{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1},\,{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-3{R}_{1}
$$

Given that $C$ has the LU factorization $C=LU,$ then $L=$
questions.worked_solution:
Applying ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-2)\cdot {R}_{1}$ and then ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-3)\cdot {R}_{1}$ is equivalent to multiplying $C$ from the left by the following elementary matrices:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{1}}\cdot C=U.
$$

Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}C=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}C & =U \\ {E}_{1}C & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ C & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ C & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ C & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ C & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}\cdot U.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
Given that
$K=[\begin{aligned}4 & 4 & 0 \\ 7 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 7 & 3\end{aligned}]$
has the LU decomposition $K=LU,$ then $L=$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $K$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $K$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}K & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 4 & 0 \\ 7 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 7 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{7}{4}){R}_{1} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -\frac{7}{4} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot K \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & -1 \\ 0 & 7 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{2} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{2}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot {E}_{1}\cdot K \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}K=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}K & =U \\ {E}_{1}K & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ K & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ K & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -\frac{7}{4} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ K & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ \frac{7}{4} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ K & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ \frac{7}{4} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}4 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
Given that 
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 2 \\ 4 & -5 & 9 \\ -3 & 0 & -5\end{aligned}]$ has the LU decomposition $A=LU,$ then ${l}_{32}\cdot {u}_{33}=$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 2 \\ 4 & -5 & 9 \\ -3 & 0 & -5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ -3 & 0 & -5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{2}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot {E}_{1}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & -6 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{2} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{3}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot {E}_{2}\cdot {E}_{1}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{3}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{3},$ ${E}_{2},$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{3}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ {E}_{2}{E}_{1}A & ={E}_{3}^{-1}U \\ {E}_{1}A & ={E}_{2}^{-1}{E}_{3}^{-1}U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}{E}_{3}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${l}_{32}=-2,$ ${u}_{33}=3,$ and ${l}_{32}\cdot {u}_{33}=-6.$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Applying ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+9\cdot {R}_{1}$ and then ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2)\cdot {R}_{1}$ is equivalent to multiplying $H$ from the left by the following elementary matrices:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 9 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{1}}\cdot H=U
$$

Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}H=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}H & =U \\ {E}_{1}H & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 9 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ H & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -9 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ H & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -9 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}\cdot U\end{aligned}
$$

Applying R2:=R2+9⋅R1 and then R3:=R3+(−2)⋅R1 is equivalent to multiplying H from the left by the following elementary matrices:

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $K$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $K$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}K & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 4 & 0 \\ 7 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 7 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{7}{4}){R}_{1} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -\frac{7}{4} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot K \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & -1 \\ 0 & 7 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{2} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{2}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot {E}_{1}\cdot K \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}K=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}K & =U \\ {E}_{1}K & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ K & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ K & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -\frac{7}{4} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ K & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ \frac{7}{4} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ K & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ \frac{7}{4} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}4 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 6 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & 2 \\ 3 & -6 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(\frac{1}{3}){R}_{1} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ \frac{1}{3} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 \\ 3 & -6 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{2}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot {E}_{1}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ {E}_{1}A & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ \frac{1}{3} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -\frac{1}{3} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -\frac{1}{3} & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}-3 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 2 \\ 4 & -5 & 9 \\ -3 & 0 & -5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ -3 & 0 & -5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{2}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot {E}_{1}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & -6 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{2} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{3}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot {E}_{2}\cdot {E}_{1}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{3}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{3},$ ${E}_{2},$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{3}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ {E}_{2}{E}_{1}A & ={E}_{3}^{-1}U \\ {E}_{1}A & ={E}_{2}^{-1}{E}_{3}^{-1}U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}{E}_{3}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${l}_{32}=-2,$ ${u}_{33}=3,$ and ${l}_{32}\cdot {u}_{33}=-6.$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Suppose that a $3\times 3$ matrix $C$ is reduced to row echelon form using the following elementary row operations, applied in the order in which they appear:

$$
{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1},\,{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-3{R}_{1}
$$

Given that $C$ has the LU factorization $C=LU,$ then $L=$
question.worked_solution:
Applying ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-2)\cdot {R}_{1}$ and then ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-3)\cdot {R}_{1}$ is equivalent to multiplying $C$ from the left by the following elementary matrices:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{1}}\cdot C=U.
$$

Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}C=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}C & =U \\ {E}_{1}C & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ C & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ C & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ C & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ C & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}\cdot U.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Suppose that a 3×3 matrix C is reduced to row echelon form using the following elementary row operations, applied in the order in which they appear: R2:=R2−2R1,R3:=R3−3R1 Given that C has the LU factorization C=LU, then L=

a
[100010321]
b
[100−210301]
c
[100−210−301]
d
[100210−301]
e
[100210301]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Applying R2:=R2+(−2)⋅R1 and then R3:=R3+(−3)⋅R1 is equivalent to multiplying C from the left by the following elementary matrices: [100010−301]⏟E2⋅[100−210001]⏟E1⋅C=U.

Now, since E2E1C=U, we can invert E2 and E1 to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

E2E1C=UE1C=E2−1UC=E1−1E2−1UC=[100−210001]−1[100010−301]−1UC=([100210001][100010301])UC=[100210301]⏟L⋅U.

last_observation.worked_solution:
Applying ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-2)\cdot {R}_{1}$ and then ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-3)\cdot {R}_{1}$ is equivalent to multiplying $C$ from the left by the following elementary matrices:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{1}}\cdot C=U.
$$

Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}C=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}C & =U \\ {E}_{1}C & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ C & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ C & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ C & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ C & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}\cdot U.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Applying R2:=R2+(−2)⋅R1 and then R3:=R3+(−3)⋅R1 is equivalent to multiplying C from the left by the following elementary matrices: [100010−301]⏟E2⋅[100−210001]⏟E1⋅C=U.

Now, since E2E1C=U, we can invert E2 and E1 to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

E2E1C=UE1C=E2−1UC=E1−1E2−1UC=[100−210001]−1[100010−301]−1UC=([100210001][100010301])UC=[100210301]⏟L⋅U.

solution.reasoning: The elimination gives U=E₂E₁C, so L=E₁⁻¹E₂⁻¹. The inverse operations add 2R₁ to R₂ and 3R₁ to R₃; hence L has first column (1,2,3) and remaining columns those of the identity. feedback.problem:
Suppose that a $3\times 3$ matrix $C$ is reduced to row echelon form using the following elementary row operations, applied in the order in which they appear:

$$
{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1},\,{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-3{R}_{1}
$$

Given that $C$ has the LU factorization $C=LU,$ then $L=$
feedback.worked_solution:
Applying ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-2)\cdot {R}_{1}$ and then ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-3)\cdot {R}_{1}$ is equivalent to multiplying $C$ from the left by the following elementary matrices:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{1}}\cdot C=U.
$$

Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}C=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}C & =U \\ {E}_{1}C & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ C & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ C & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ C & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ C & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}\cdot U.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
Suppose that a $3\times 3$ matrix $H$ is reduced to row echelon form using the following elementary row operations, applied in the order in which they appear:

$$
{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+9{R}_{1},\,{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-2{R}_{1}.
$$

Given that $H$ has the LU factorization $H=LU,$ then $L=$
question.worked_solution:
Applying ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+9\cdot {R}_{1}$ and then ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2)\cdot {R}_{1}$ is equivalent to multiplying $H$ from the left by the following elementary matrices:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 9 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{1}}\cdot H=U
$$

Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}H=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}H & =U \\ {E}_{1}H & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 9 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ H & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -9 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ H & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -9 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}\cdot U\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Suppose that a 3×3 matrix H is reduced to row echelon form using the following elementary row operations, applied in the order in which they appear: R2:=R2+9R1,R3:=R3−2R1. Given that H has the LU factorization H=LU, then L=

a
[100910−201]
b
[100010−291]
c
[1000102−91]
d
[100−910201]
e
[100910001]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Applying R2:=R2+9⋅R1 and then R3:=R3+(−2)⋅R1 is equivalent to multiplying H from the left by the following elementary matrices:

[100010−201]⏟E2⋅[100910001]⏟E1⋅H=U

Now, since E2E1H=U, we can invert E2 and E1 to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

E2E1H=UE1H=E2−1UH=E1−1E2−1UH=[100910001]−1[100010−201]−1UH=([100−910001][100010201])UH=[100−910201]⏟L⋅U

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 9 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{1}}\cdot H=U
$$

Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}H=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$

Question 2
?

Suppose that a 3×3 matrix H is reduced to row echelon form using the following elementary row operations, applied in the order in which they appear: R2:=R2+9R1,R3:=R3−2R1. Given that H has the LU factorization H=LU, then L=

a
[100910−201]
b
[100010−291]
c
[1000102−91]
d
[100−910201]
e
[100910001]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Applying R2:=R2+9⋅R1 and then R3:=R3+(−2)⋅R1 is equivalent to multiplying H from the left by the following elementary matrices:

[100010−201]⏟E2⋅[100910001]⏟E1⋅H=U

Now, since E2E1H=U, we can invert E2 and E1 to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

E2E1H=UE1H=E2−1UH=E1−1E2−1UH=[100910001]−1[100010−201]−1UH=([100−910001][100010201])UH=[100−910201]⏟L⋅U

solution.reasoning: L reverses the elimination operations: subtract 9 times row 1 from row 2 and add 2 times row 1 to row 3. Thus its diagonal entries are 1, with L₂₁=-9 and L₃₁=2, giving option d. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key.

feedback.problem:
Suppose that a $3\times 3$ matrix $H$ is reduced to row echelon form using the following elementary row operations, applied in the order in which they appear:

$$
{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+9{R}_{1},\,{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-2{R}_{1}.
$$

Given that $H$ has the LU factorization $H=LU,$ then $L=$
feedback.worked_solution:
Applying ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+9\cdot {R}_{1}$ and then ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2)\cdot {R}_{1}$ is equivalent to multiplying $H$ from the left by the following elementary matrices:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 9 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{E}_{1}}\cdot H=U
$$

Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}H=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}H & =U \\ {E}_{1}H & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ H & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 9 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ H & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -9 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ H & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -9 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}\cdot U\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Given that
$K=[\begin{aligned}4 & 4 & 0 \\ 7 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 7 & 3\end{aligned}]$
has the LU decomposition $K=LU,$ then $L=$
question.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $K$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $K$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}K & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 4 & 0 \\ 7 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 7 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{7}{4}){R}_{1} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -\frac{7}{4} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot K \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & -1 \\ 0 & 7 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{2} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{2}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot {E}_{1}\cdot K \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}K=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}K & =U \\ {E}_{1}K & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ K & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ K & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -\frac{7}{4} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ K & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ \frac{7}{4} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ K & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ \frac{7}{4} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}4 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the matrices L and U, we reduce the matrix K to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to K in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

last_observation.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $K$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $K$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}K & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 4 & 0 \\ 7 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 7 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{7}{4}){R}_{1} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -\frac{7}{4} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot K \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & -1 \\ 0 & 7 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{2} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{2}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot {E}_{1}\cdot K \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}K=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}K & =U \\ {E}_{1}K & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ K & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ K & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -\frac{7}{4} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ K & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ \frac{7}{4} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ K & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ \frac{7}{4} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}4 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$
