last_observation.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 6 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & 2 \\ 3 & -6 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(\frac{1}{3}){R}_{1} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ \frac{1}{3} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 \\ 3 & -6 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{2}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot {E}_{1}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{2}{E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{2}$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ {E}_{1}A & ={E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ \frac{1}{3} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -\frac{1}{3} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -\frac{1}{3} & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}-3 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Given that A=[1−224−59−30−5] has the LU decomposition A=LU, then l32⋅u33=

a
−4
b
−6
c
6
d
−9
e
4
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the matrices L and U, we reduce the matrix A to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to A in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

A=[1−224−59−30−5]R2:=R2+(−4)R1⟺[100−410001]⏞E1⋅A∼[1−22031−30−5]R3:=R3+3R1⟺[100010301]⏞E2⋅E1⋅A∼[1−220310−61]R3:=R3+2R2⟺[100010021]⏞E3⋅E2⋅E1⋅A∼[1−22031003]=U

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix U. Now, since E3E2E1A=U, we can invert E3, E2, and E1 to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

E3E2E1A=UE2E1A=E3−1UE1A=E2−1E3−1UA=E1−1E2−1E3−1UA=[100−410001]−1[100010301]−1[100010021]−1UA=([100410001][100010−301][1000100−21])UA=[100410−3−21]⏟L[1−22031003]⏟U

Therefore, l32=−2, u33=3, and l32⋅u33=−6.

solution.reasoning: Using unit-diagonal L, eliminate column 1: R₂−4R₁=(0,3,1) and R₃+3R₁=(0,−6,1). Thus l₃₂=−6/3=−2. The operation R₃+2R₂ gives (0,0,3), so u₃₃=3 and l₃₂u₃₃=−6, option b. No Math Academy answer or grade is captured.

feedback.problem:
Given that 
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 2 \\ 4 & -5 & 9 \\ -3 & 0 & -5\end{aligned}]$ has the LU decomposition $A=LU,$ then ${l}_{32}\cdot {u}_{33}=$
feedback.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 2 \\ 4 & -5 & 9 \\ -3 & 0 & -5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ -3 & 0 & -5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{2}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot {E}_{1}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & -6 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{2} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{3}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot {E}_{2}\cdot {E}_{1}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{3}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{3},$ ${E}_{2},$ and ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{3}{E}_{2}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ {E}_{2}{E}_{1}A & ={E}_{3}^{-1}U \\ {E}_{1}A & ={E}_{2}^{-1}{E}_{3}^{-1}U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}{E}_{2}^{-1}{E}_{3}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & =([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}])U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${l}_{32}=-2,$ ${u}_{33}=3,$ and ${l}_{32}\cdot {u}_{33}=-6.$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: What is the range of the function $f(x)=-\frac{1}{3}(x+2)(x-2)?$
questions.worked_solution:
The given parabola is written in factored form,

$$
y=a(x-{x}_{1})(x-{x}_{2}),
$$

with $a=-\frac{1}{3}<0.$ 

Because the leading coefficient is negative, the parabola opens downward. Consequently, there is no minimum output, and the vertex corresponds to the maximum output.

The two roots of the parabola are ${x}_{1}=-2$ and ${x}_{2}=2,$ and we can find the $x$-coordinate of the vertex by taking the average of the roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}}{2}=\frac{-2+2}{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $x=0$ back into the function to find the $y$-value of the vertex:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{1}{3}(x+2)(x-2) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}(0+2)(0-2) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\cdot 2\cdot (-2) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertex is $(0,\frac{4}{3}),$ and the range of the function is $(-\infty ,\frac{4}{3}].$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: What is the range of the function $f(x)=-{x}^{2}+6x-8?$
questions.worked_solution:
The given parabola is written in standard form,

$$
y=a{x}^{2}+bx+c,
$$

with $a=-1<0,$ $b=6,$ and $c=-8.$

Because the leading coefficient is negative, the parabola opens downward. Consequently, there is no minimum output, and the vertex corresponds to the maximum output.

The $x$-coordinate of the vertex is given by

$$
x=-\frac{b}{2a}=-\frac{6}{2\cdot (-1)}=3.
$$

Now, we substitute $x=3$ back into the function to find the $y$-value of the vertex:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-{x}^{2}+6x-8 \\  & =-(3)^{2}+6(3)-8 \\  & =-9+18-8 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertex is $(3,1),$ and the range of the function is $(-\infty ,1].$

questions.problem: What is the range of the function $f(x)=-3(x+1)^{2}-7?$

$$

$$

where $a$ is the leading coefficient and $(h,k)$ is the vertex. 

- Since $h=-1$ and $k=-7,$ the vertex is $(-1,-7).$

- Since $a=-3<0,$ the parabola opens downwards.

Because the parabola opens downwards, there is no minimum output, and the vertex corresponds to the maximum output. 

Therefore, the range is $(-\infty ,-7].$

The given parabola is written in factored form,

$$
y=a(x-{x}_{1})(x-{x}_{2}),
$$

with $a=-\frac{1}{3}<0.$ 

Because the leading coefficient is negative, the parabola opens downward. Consequently, there is no minimum output, and the vertex corresponds to the maximum output.

The two roots of the parabola are ${x}_{1}=-2$ and ${x}_{2}=2,$ and we can find the $x$-coordinate of the vertex by taking the average of the roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}}{2}=\frac{-2+2}{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $x=0$ back into the function to find the $y$-value of the vertex:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{1}{3}(x+2)(x-2) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}(0+2)(0-2) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\cdot 2\cdot (-2) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertex is $(0,\frac{4}{3}),$ and the range of the function is $(-\infty ,\frac{4}{3}].$

$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The given parabola is written in factored form,

$$
y=a(x-{x}_{1})(x-{x}_{2}),
$$

with $a=-1<0.$ 

Because the leading coefficient is negative, the parabola opens downward. Consequently, there is no minimum output, and the vertex corresponds to the maximum output.

The two roots of the parabola are ${x}_{1}=-9$ and ${x}_{2}=-7,$ and we can find the $x$-coordinate of the vertex by taking the average of the roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}}{2}=\frac{-9-7}{2}=-8\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $x=-8$ back into the function to find the $y$-value of the vertex:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-(x+7)(x+9) \\  & =-(-8+7)(-8+9) \\  & =-(-1)\cdot 1 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertex is $(-8,1),$ and the range of the function is $(-\infty ,1],$ i.e. $-\infty <f(x)\le 1.$

$$
y=a(x-{x}_{1})(x-{x}_{2}),
$$

with $a=-\frac{1}{3}<0.$ 

Because the leading coefficient is negative, the parabola opens downward. Consequently, there is no minimum output, and the vertex corresponds to the maximum output.

The two roots of the parabola are ${x}_{1}=-2$ and ${x}_{2}=2,$ and we can find the $x$-coordinate of the vertex by taking the average of the roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}}{2}=\frac{-2+2}{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $x=0$ back into the function to find the $y$-value of the vertex:

$$

$$

Therefore, the vertex is $(0,\frac{4}{3}),$ and the range of the function is $(-\infty ,\frac{4}{3}].$

question.html:
Question 1
?

What is the range of the function f(x)=−13(x+2)(x−2)?

a
[43,∞)
b
(−∞,43]
c
[−43,∞)
d
(−∞,−43]
e
(−∞,13]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The given parabola is written in factored form,

y=a(x−x1)(x−x2),

with a=−13<0.

Because the leading coefficient is negative, the parabola opens downward. Consequently, there is no minimum output, and the vertex corresponds to the maximum output.

The two roots of the parabola are x1=−2 and x2=2, and we can find the x-coordinate of the vertex by taking the average of the roots: x=x1+x22=−2+22=0

Then, we substitute x=0 back into the function to find the y-value of the vertex: y=−13(x+2)(x−2)=−13(0+2)(0−2)=−13⋅2⋅(−2)=43

Therefore, the vertex is (0,43), and the range of the function is (−∞,43].

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.worked_solution:
The given parabola is written in factored form,

$$
y=a(x-{x}_{1})(x-{x}_{2}),
$$

with $a=-\frac{1}{3}<0.$ 

Because the leading coefficient is negative, the parabola opens downward. Consequently, there is no minimum output, and the vertex corresponds to the maximum output.

The two roots of the parabola are ${x}_{1}=-2$ and ${x}_{2}=2,$ and we can find the $x$-coordinate of the vertex by taking the average of the roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}}{2}=\frac{-2+2}{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $x=0$ back into the function to find the $y$-value of the vertex:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{1}{3}(x+2)(x-2) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}(0+2)(0-2) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\cdot 2\cdot (-2) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertex is $(0,\frac{4}{3}),$ and the range of the function is $(-\infty ,\frac{4}{3}].$

question.html:
Question 1
?

What is the range of the function f(x)=−13(x+2)(x−2)?

a
[43,∞)
b
(−∞,43]
c
[−43,∞)
d
(−∞,−43]
e
(−∞,13]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The given parabola is written in factored form,

y=a(x−x1)(x−x2),

with a=−13<0.

Because the leading coefficient is negative, the parabola opens downward. Consequently, there is no minimum output, and the vertex corresponds to the maximum output.

The two roots of the parabola are x1=−2 and x2=2, and we can find the x-coordinate of the vertex by taking the average of the roots: x=x1+x22=−2+22=0

Then, we substitute x=0 back into the function to find the y-value of the vertex: y=−13(x+2)(x−2)=−13(0+2)(0−2)=−13⋅2⋅(−2)=43

Therefore, the vertex is (0,43), and the range of the function is (−∞,43].

solution.reasoning: Expanding gives f(x)=-x^2/3+4/3. Since x^2≥0, the maximum is 4/3, attained at x=0; the function is unbounded below. Thus the range is (-∞,4/3], choice b. No Math Academy answer or grade evidence is captured.

feedback.problem: What is the range of the function $f(x)=-\frac{1}{3}(x+2)(x-2)?$
feedback.worked_solution:
The given parabola is written in factored form,

$$
y=a(x-{x}_{1})(x-{x}_{2}),
$$

with $a=-\frac{1}{3}<0.$ 

Because the leading coefficient is negative, the parabola opens downward. Consequently, there is no minimum output, and the vertex corresponds to the maximum output.

The two roots of the parabola are ${x}_{1}=-2$ and ${x}_{2}=2,$ and we can find the $x$-coordinate of the vertex by taking the average of the roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}}{2}=\frac{-2+2}{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $x=0$ back into the function to find the $y$-value of the vertex:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{1}{3}(x+2)(x-2) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}(0+2)(0-2) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\cdot 2\cdot (-2) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertex is $(0,\frac{4}{3}),$ and the range of the function is $(-\infty ,\frac{4}{3}].$

question.problem: What is the range of the function $f(x)=-{x}^{2}+6x-8?$
question.worked_solution:
The given parabola is written in standard form,

$$
y=a{x}^{2}+bx+c,
$$

with $a=-1<0,$ $b=6,$ and $c=-8.$

Because the leading coefficient is negative, the parabola opens downward. Consequently, there is no minimum output, and the vertex corresponds to the maximum output.

The $x$-coordinate of the vertex is given by

$$
x=-\frac{b}{2a}=-\frac{6}{2\cdot (-1)}=3.
$$

Now, we substitute $x=3$ back into the function to find the $y$-value of the vertex:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-{x}^{2}+6x-8 \\  & =-(3)^{2}+6(3)-8 \\  & =-9+18-8 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertex is $(3,1),$ and the range of the function is $(-\infty ,1].$

last_observation.worked_solution:
The given parabola is written in standard form,

$$
y=a{x}^{2}+bx+c,
$$

with $a=-1<0,$ $b=6,$ and $c=-8.$

Because the leading coefficient is negative, the parabola opens downward. Consequently, there is no minimum output, and the vertex corresponds to the maximum output.

The $x$-coordinate of the vertex is given by

$$
x=-\frac{b}{2a}=-\frac{6}{2\cdot (-1)}=3.
$$

Now, we substitute $x=3$ back into the function to find the $y$-value of the vertex:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-{x}^{2}+6x-8 \\  & =-(3)^{2}+6(3)-8 \\  & =-9+18-8 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertex is $(3,1),$ and the range of the function is $(-\infty ,1].$

The parabola is written in vertex form, 

$$
y=a(x-h)^{2}+k,
$$

where $a$ is the leading coefficient and $(h,k)$ is the vertex. 

- Since $h=-1$ and $k=-7,$ the vertex is $(-1,-7).$

- Since $a=-3<0,$ the parabola opens downwards.

Because the parabola opens downwards, there is no minimum output, and the vertex corresponds to the maximum output. 

Therefore, the range is $(-\infty ,-7].$

question.name: Question 5
question.worked_solution:
The given parabola is written in factored form,

$$
y=a(x-{x}_{1})(x-{x}_{2}),
$$

with $a=-1<0.$ 

Because the leading coefficient is negative, the parabola opens downward. Consequently, there is no minimum output, and the vertex corresponds to the maximum output.

The two roots of the parabola are ${x}_{1}=-9$ and ${x}_{2}=-7,$ and we can find the $x$-coordinate of the vertex by taking the average of the roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}}{2}=\frac{-9-7}{2}=-8\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $x=-8$ back into the function to find the $y$-value of the vertex:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-(x+7)(x+9) \\  & =-(-8+7)(-8+9) \\  & =-(-1)\cdot 1 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertex is $(-8,1),$ and the range of the function is $(-\infty ,1],$ i.e. $-\infty <f(x)\le 1.$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.worked_solution:
Computing the first derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(x) & ={(-{x}^{3}+4x\sqrt{x})}^{′} \\  & ={(-{x}^{3}+4{x}^{3/2})}^{′} \\  & =3(-{x}^{2})+\frac{3}{2}(4{x}^{1/2}) \\  & =-3{x}^{2}+6{x}^{1/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the second derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{″}(x) & ={(-3{x}^{2}+6{x}^{1/2})}^{′} \\  & =2(-3x)+\frac{1}{2}(6{x}^{-1/2}) \\  & =-6x+3{x}^{-1/2} \\  & =-6x+\frac{3}{\sqrt{x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the second derivative at $x=1$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{″}(1) & =-6(1)+\frac{3}{\sqrt{1}} \\  & =-6+3 \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}$ for $y=7x-4{x}^{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Computing the first derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(7x-4{x}^{2}) \\  & =7-2\cdot 4x \\  & =7-8x.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the second derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(7-8x) \\  & =0-8 \\  & =-8.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.worked_solution:
Computing the first derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{6{x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}-8}{2x}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{x}^{2}+x-4{x}^{-1}) \\  & =6x+1+(-1)(-4{x}^{-2}) \\  & =6x+1+4{x}^{-2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the second derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6x+1+4{x}^{-2}) \\  & =6+0+(-2)(4{x}^{-3}) \\  & =6-\frac{8}{{x}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can rewrite the function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{5-{x}^{4}}{6{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{5}{6{x}^{2}}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the first derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{5}{6{x}^{2}}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{6}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{5}{6}{x}^{-2}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{6}) \\  & =-\frac{5}{3}{x}^{-3}-\frac{x}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the second derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-\frac{5}{3}{x}^{-3}-\frac{x}{3}) \\  & =5{x}^{-4}-\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, computing the third derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{‴}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(5{x}^{-4}-\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =-20{x}^{-5} \\  & =-\frac{20}{{x}^{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

                    Computing Second Order Derivatives
canonical_examples.problem: Find $f''(x)$ for $f(x) = 2x^3 + \dfrac 1 x.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Computing the first derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={(2{x}^{3}+\frac{1}{x})}^{′} \\  & ={(2{x}^{3}+{x}^{-1})}^{′} \\  & =2(3){x}^{2}-{x}^{-2} \\  & =6{x}^{2}-{x}^{-2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the second derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =(6{x}^{2}-{x}^{-2})^{′} \\  & =6(2)x-(-2){x}^{-3} \\  & =12x+2{x}^{-3}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Calculate $\dfrac {\textrm d^2 y}{\textrm d x^2}$ for $y = 3 x^4 + 5x+ \sqrt x.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Computing the first derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{x}^{4}+5x+\sqrt{x}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{x}^{4}+5x+{x}^{1/2}) \\  & =3(4){x}^{3}+5+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2} \\  & =12{x}^{3}+5+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the second derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(12{x}^{3}+5+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2}) \\  & =12(3){x}^{2}+0+\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{1}{2}){x}^{-3/2} \\  & =36{x}^{2}-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{-3/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Example: 
                    Computing Higher Order Derivatives
canonical_examples.problem: Given $y = \dfrac {3 x^2 + x - 1} x$, find $\dfrac {\textrm d^{3} y} {\textrm d x^3}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can rewrite the function as the sum of powers of $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{3{x}^{2}+x-1}{x} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}}{x}+\frac{x}{x}-\frac{1}{x} \\  & =3x+1-{x}^{-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the first derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3x+1-{x}^{-1}) \\  & =3+0-(-1){x}^{-2} \\  & =3+{x}^{-2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the second derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3+{x}^{-2}) \\  & =0+(-2){x}^{-3} \\  & =-2{x}^{-3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, computing the third derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{3}y}{\text{d}{x}^{3}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-2{x}^{-3}) \\  & =-2(-3){x}^{-4} \\  & =6{x}^{-4}.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
The **second derivative**  is the derivative of a function's first derivative. It is written as $f''(x).$

To calculate the second derivative of a function $f(x)$, we first need to calculate the first derivative $f'(x).$ After that, we calculate the derivative of $f'(x).$ So using prime $\left('\right)$ notation, we can define the second derivative of a function $f(x)$ as

$$
f''(x) = (f'(x))'.
$$

Let's try it out with the function $f(x) = 4x^2 + 3x.$ The first derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =(4{x}^{2}+3x)^{′} \\  & =4(2)x+3 \\  & =8x+3.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now calculate the derivative of $f'(x)$ to give us $f''(x).$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =({f}^{′}(x))^{′} \\  & =(8x+3)^{′} \\  & =8+0 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  the second derivative of $f(x)$ is $8.$

tutorials.name: Using Leibniz Notation
tutorials.problem:
We can also express the second derivative using $\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d} x}$ notation, also known as Leibniz notation. If we have a function $f(x),$ then the second derivative $f''(x)$ can be written as

$$
f''(x) = \dfrac {\textrm d^2 f}{\textrm d x^2} = \dfrac {\textrm d} {\textrm d x}\left(\dfrac {\textrm df} {\textrm d x}\right).
$$

Sometimes, we define a function as $y=f(x),$ in which case we could also express the second derivative as $\dfrac {\textrm d^2 y}{\textrm d x^2}.$

tutorials.name: Higher Order Derivatives
tutorials.problem:
To calculate the third derivative of the function $f(x)=2x^4+3x,$ we need to differentiate it three times.

Computing the first derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{4}+3x) \\  & =2\cdot 4{x}^{4-1}+1\cdot 3{x}^{1-1} \\ \text{ } & =8{x}^{3}+3{x}^{0} \\  & =8{x}^{3}+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the second derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(8{x}^{3}+3) \\  & =8\cdot 3{x}^{3-1}+0 \\ \text{ } & =24{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, computing the third derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{‴}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(24{x}^{2}) \\  & =24\cdot 2{x}^{2-1} \\ \text{ } & =48x.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the third derivative of $f(x)$ is $f'''(x)=48x.$ 

Using Leibniz notation, the third derivative of a function $f(x)$ can also be written as

$$
f'''(x)=\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d x}\left(\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d x}\left(\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d x}(f(x))\right)\right)=\dfrac {\textrm d^3}{\textrm d x^3}f(x).
$$

In general, if we want to calculate the $n$-th order derivative of a function, we need to differentiate it $n$ times:

$$
f^{(n)}(x)=\dfrac {\textrm d^n}{\textrm d x^n}f(x).
$$

**Note**: The parenthesis in the superscript of $f^{(n)}(x)$ means that it is the the $n$-th derivative of $f(x).$ This is to distinguish it from $f^n(x)$ with no parenthesis, which indicates the $n$-th power of $f(x).$

tutorial.problem:
We can also express the second derivative using $\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d} x}$ notation, also known as Leibniz notation. If we have a function $f(x),$ then the second derivative $f''(x)$ can be written as

$$
f''(x) = \dfrac {\textrm d^2 f}{\textrm d x^2} = \dfrac {\textrm d} {\textrm d x}\left(\dfrac {\textrm df} {\textrm d x}\right).
$$

Sometimes, we define a function as $y=f(x),$ in which case we could also express the second derivative as $\dfrac {\textrm d^2 y}{\textrm d x^2}.$

tutorial.name: Higher Order Derivatives
tutorial.problem:
To calculate the third derivative of the function $f(x)=2x^4+3x,$ we need to differentiate it three times.

Computing the first derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{4}+3x) \\  & =2\cdot 4{x}^{4-1}+1\cdot 3{x}^{1-1} \\ \text{ } & =8{x}^{3}+3{x}^{0} \\  & =8{x}^{3}+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the second derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(8{x}^{3}+3) \\  & =8\cdot 3{x}^{3-1}+0 \\ \text{ } & =24{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, computing the third derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{‴}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(24{x}^{2}) \\  & =24\cdot 2{x}^{2-1} \\ \text{ } & =48x.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the third derivative of $f(x)$ is $f'''(x)=48x.$ 

Using Leibniz notation, the third derivative of a function $f(x)$ can also be written as

$$
f'''(x)=\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d x}\left(\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d x}\left(\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d x}(f(x))\right)\right)=\dfrac {\textrm d^3}{\textrm d x^3}f(x).
$$

In general, if we want to calculate the $n$-th order derivative of a function, we need to differentiate it $n$ times:

$$
f^{(n)}(x)=\dfrac {\textrm d^n}{\textrm d x^n}f(x).
$$

**Note**: The parenthesis in the superscript of $f^{(n)}(x)$ means that it is the the $n$-th derivative of $f(x).$ This is to distinguish it from $f^n(x)$ with no parenthesis, which indicates the $n$-th power of $f(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(x) & ={(-{x}^{3}+4x\sqrt{x})}^{′} \\  & ={(-{x}^{3}+4{x}^{3/2})}^{′} \\  & =3(-{x}^{2})+\frac{3}{2}(4{x}^{1/2}) \\  & =-3{x}^{2}+6{x}^{1/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the second derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{″}(x) & ={(-3{x}^{2}+6{x}^{1/2})}^{′} \\  & =2(-3x)+\frac{1}{2}(6{x}^{-1/2}) \\  & =-6x+3{x}^{-1/2} \\  & =-6x+\frac{3}{\sqrt{x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the second derivative at $x=1$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{″}(1) & =-6(1)+\frac{3}{\sqrt{1}} \\  & =-6+3 \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: Calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}$ for $y=7x-4{x}^{2}.$
question.worked_solution:
Computing the first derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(7x-4{x}^{2}) \\  & =7-2\cdot 4x \\  & =7-8x.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the second derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(7-8x) \\  & =0-8 \\  & =-8.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Computing the first derivative, we get

dydx=ddx(7x−4x2)=7−2⋅4x=7−8x.

Computing the second derivative, we get

d2ydx2=ddx(7−8x)=0−8=−8.

question.name: Question 4
question.worked_solution:
Computing the first derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{6{x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}-8}{2x}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{x}^{2}+x-4{x}^{-1}) \\  & =6x+1+(-1)(-4{x}^{-2}) \\  & =6x+1+4{x}^{-2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the second derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6x+1+4{x}^{-2}) \\  & =6+0+(-2)(4{x}^{-3}) \\  & =6-\frac{8}{{x}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can rewrite the function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{5-{x}^{4}}{6{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{5}{6{x}^{2}}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the first derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{5}{6{x}^{2}}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{6}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{5}{6}{x}^{-2}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{6}) \\  & =-\frac{5}{3}{x}^{-3}-\frac{x}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the second derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-\frac{5}{3}{x}^{-3}-\frac{x}{3}) \\  & =5{x}^{-4}-\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, computing the third derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{‴}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(5{x}^{-4}-\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =-20{x}^{-5} \\  & =-\frac{20}{{x}^{5}}.\end{aligned}

Question 5
?

Given f(x)=5−x46x2, find f‴(x).

a
−10x4−x3
b
1−203x5
c
−20x5
d
5x4−13
e
−53x3−13
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that we can rewrite the function as follows:

f(x)=5−x46x2=56x2−x26

Now, computing the first derivative, we get f′(x)=ddx(56x2−x26)=ddx(56x−2−x26)=−53x−3−x3.

Computing the second derivative, we get f″(x)=ddx(−53x−3−x3)=5x−4−13.

Finally, computing the third derivative, we get f‴(x)=ddx(5x−4−13)=−20x−5=−20x5.

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{5}{6{x}^{2}}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{6}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{5}{6}{x}^{-2}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{6}) \\  & =-\frac{5}{3}{x}^{-3}-\frac{x}{3}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-\frac{5}{3}{x}^{-3}-\frac{x}{3}) \\  & =5{x}^{-4}-\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Question 5
?

Given f(x)=5−x46x2, find f‴(x).

a
−10x4−x3
b
1−203x5
c
−20x5
d
5x4−13
e
−53x3−13
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that we can rewrite the function as follows:

f(x)=5−x46x2=56x2−x26

Now, computing the first derivative, we get f′(x)=ddx(56x2−x26)=ddx(56x−2−x26)=−53x−3−x3.

Computing the second derivative, we get f″(x)=ddx(−53x−3−x3)=5x−4−13.

Finally, computing the third derivative, we get f‴(x)=ddx(5x−4−13)=−20x−5=−20x5.
question.knowledge_point: Computing Higher Order Derivatives

solution.reasoning: Rewrite f(x)=(5/6)x^{-2}-(1/6)x^2 for x≠0. Then f'(x)=-(5/3)x^{-3}-x/3, f''(x)=5x^{-4}-1/3, and f'''(x)=-20x^{-5}, matching option c. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key for this question.

feedback.name: Question 5
feedback.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can rewrite the function as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{5-{x}^{4}}{6{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{5}{6{x}^{2}}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the first derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{5}{6{x}^{2}}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{6}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{5}{6}{x}^{-2}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{6}) \\  & =-\frac{5}{3}{x}^{-3}-\frac{x}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the second derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-\frac{5}{3}{x}^{-3}-\frac{x}{3}) \\  & =5{x}^{-4}-\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, computing the third derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{‴}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(5{x}^{-4}-\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =-20{x}^{-5} \\  & =-\frac{20}{{x}^{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the first derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x+3x) \\  & =x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the second derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3) \\  & =1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, computing the third derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{‴}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

f‴(x)=
−cosx
.
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Computing the first derivative, we get f′(x)=ddx(12x2+sin⁡x+3x)=x+cos⁡x+3.

Computing the second derivative, we get

f″(x)=ddx(x+cos⁡x+3)=1−sin⁡x.

Finally, computing the third derivative, we get f‴(x)=ddx(1−sin⁡x)=−cos⁡x.

What are the equations of the horizontal asymptotes of $y=f(x)$ whose graph is shown above?
questions.worked_solution:
- On the right of the graph, we see that as $x$ gets larger and larger, the function $f(x)$ levels off to the value of $-3.$ We can express this as follows:

$$
f(x)\to -3\,\text{as}\,x\to \infty 
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ has a horizontal asymptote at $y=-3.$

- On the left of the graph, we see that as $x$ gets more and more negative, the function $f(x)$ levels off to the value of $2.$ We can express this as follows:

$$
f(x)\to 2\,\text{as}\,x\to -\infty 
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ also has a horizontal asymptote at $y=2.$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14250658/assets/7471044234ec20534f33abb45d26db3c0a2876bed0fcc73844d1867b354491c0.png)

Which of the following statements are true for the graph shown above?

I. $f(x)\to 2$ as $x\to -\infty $

II. $f(x)\to 1$ as $x\to \infty $

III. $f(x)\to 0$ as $x\to -\infty $
questions.worked_solution:
Let's analyze each statement one-by-one.

- On the left of the graph, we see that as $x$ gets more and more negative, the function $f(x)$ levels off to the value of $2.$ We can express this as follows:

$$
f(x)\to 2\,\text{as}\,x\to -\infty 
$$

Therefore, statement I is true while statement III is false.

- On the right of the graph, we see that as $x$ gets larger and larger, the function $f(x)$ levels off to the value of $1.$ We can express this as follows:

$$
f(x)\to 1\,\text{as}\,x\to \infty 
$$

Therefore, statement II is true.

As a result, the correct answer is "I and II only".

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14250658/assets/c12deadd41a9c2853d0d2d50ba5c19ac6ca13012d7672941c92fa5e6cc5df642.png)

Which of the following statements are true for the graph shown above?

I. $y=-1$ is a horizontal asymptote of $f(x)$

II. $y=1$ is a horizontal asymptote of $f(x)$

III. $y=2$ is a horizontal asymptote of $f(x)$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's analyze each statement one-by-one.

- On the right of the graph, we see that as $x$ gets larger and larger, the function $f(x)$ levels off to the value of $1.$ We can express this as follows:

$$
f(x)\to 1\,\text{as}\,x\to \infty 
$$

This means that $y=1$ is a horizontal asymptote of $f(x).$ Therefore, statement II is true.

- On the left of the graph, we see that as $x$ gets more and more negative, the function $f(x)$ levels off to the value of $2.$ We can express this as follows:

$$
f(x)\to 2\,\text{as}\,x\to -\infty .
$$

This means that $y=2$ is a horizontal asymptote of $f(x).$ Therefore, III is also true.

- The horizontal asymptotes of $f(x)$ are $y=1$ and $y=2.$ The line $y=-1$ is not a horizontal asymptote of $f(x)$ because the function does not level off to $-1$ on the right nor on the left. Therefore, I is false.

As a result, the correct answer is "II and III only".

question.html:
Question 1
?

What are the equations of the horizontal asymptotes of y=f(x) whose graph is shown above?

a
x=−3 and x=1
b
x=−3 and x=2
c
The function has no horizontal asymptotes
d
y=−3 and y=2
e
y=−3 and y=1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

  • On the right of the graph, we see that as x gets larger and larger, the function f(x) levels off to the value of −3. We can express this as follows: f(x)→−3asx→∞ Therefore, f(x) has a horizontal asymptote at y=−3.

  • On the left of the graph, we see that as x gets more and more negative, the function f(x) levels off to the value of 2. We can express this as follows: f(x)→2asx→−∞ Therefore, f(x) also has a horizontal asymptote at y=2.

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.worked_solution:
On the right of the graph, we see that as $x$ gets larger and larger, the function $f(x)$ levels off to the value of $1.$ We can express this as follows:

$$
f(x)\to 1\,\text{as}\,x\to \infty 
$$

Therefore, $a=1.$

observed_steps.worked_solution:

$$
f(x)\to 1\,\text{as}\,x\to \infty 
$$

This means that $y=1$ is a horizontal asymptote of $f(x).$ Therefore, statement II is true.

- On the left of the graph, we see that as $x$ gets more and more negative, the function $f(x)$ levels off to the value of $2.$ We can express this as follows:

$$
f(x)\to 2\,\text{as}\,x\to -\infty .

As a result, the correct answer is "II and III only".

Which of the following statements are true for the graph shown above?

I. $f(x)\to 2$ as $x\to -\infty $

II. $f(x)\to 1$ as $x\to \infty $

III. $f(x)\to 0$ as $x\to -\infty $
question.worked_solution:
Let's analyze each statement one-by-one.

- On the left of the graph, we see that as $x$ gets more and more negative, the function $f(x)$ levels off to the value of $2.$ We can express this as follows:

$$
f(x)\to 2\,\text{as}\,x\to -\infty 
$$

Therefore, statement I is true while statement III is false.

- On the right of the graph, we see that as $x$ gets larger and larger, the function $f(x)$ levels off to the value of $1.$ We can express this as follows:

$$
f(x)\to 1\,\text{as}\,x\to \infty 
$$

Therefore, statement II is true.

As a result, the correct answer is "I and II only".

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14250658/assets/c12deadd41a9c2853d0d2d50ba5c19ac6ca13012d7672941c92fa5e6cc5df642.png)

Which of the following statements are true for the graph shown above?

I. $y=-1$ is a horizontal asymptote of $f(x)$

II. $y=1$ is a horizontal asymptote of $f(x)$

III. $y=2$ is a horizontal asymptote of $f(x)$
question.worked_solution:
Let's analyze each statement one-by-one.

- On the right of the graph, we see that as $x$ gets larger and larger, the function $f(x)$ levels off to the value of $1.$ We can express this as follows:

$$
f(x)\to 1\,\text{as}\,x\to \infty 
$$

This means that $y=1$ is a horizontal asymptote of $f(x).$ Therefore, statement II is true.

- On the left of the graph, we see that as $x$ gets more and more negative, the function $f(x)$ levels off to the value of $2.$ We can express this as follows:

$$
f(x)\to 2\,\text{as}\,x\to -\infty .
$$

This means that $y=2$ is a horizontal asymptote of $f(x).$ Therefore, III is also true.

- The horizontal asymptotes of $f(x)$ are $y=1$ and $y=2.$ The line $y=-1$ is not a horizontal asymptote of $f(x)$ because the function does not level off to $-1$ on the right nor on the left. Therefore, I is false.

As a result, the correct answer is "II and III only".

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Which of the following curves is generated by $y=-3(x+2)(x+1)(x-1)?$

(*Note: Figures not drawn to scale*)
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that the function is a product of $3$ linear binomials, so this function is a cubic function. Moreover, it is a negative cubic because if we were to expand the parentheses, the coefficient of the ${x}^{3}$ term would be negative:

$$
-3(x+2)(x+1)(x-1)=-3x\cdot x\cdot x+⋯=-3{x}^{3}+⋯
$$

The equation is given in the factored form. So by the zero-product rule, we deduce that the roots are  $x=-2,$ $x=-1,$ and $x=1.$ 

We now find the $y$-intercept of the curve by plugging the value $x=0$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-3(0+2)(0+1)(0-1) \\  & =-3(2)(1)(-1) \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we draw an $\text{S}$-shaped graph that passes through the three roots $x=-2,-1,1$ and has the $y$-intercept $y=6,$ as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14250730/assets/472cf0dd7807c15e8e8334a163d1cfbfbbdcd974534e99b94222929048e72b31.png)

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
Given that $x=2$ is a root of $f(x)=-{x}^{3}+7{x}^{2}-14x+8,$ which of the following curves is generated by $y=f(x)?$

(*Note: Figures not drawn to scale*)
questions.worked_solution:
First, we notice that the function is a negative cubic curve because the coefficient of ${x}^{3}$ is negative.

We are told that $x=2$ is a root of $f(x),$ which means that $(x-2)$ is a factor of $f(x).$ So, to find the other roots of $f(x)$ we use synthetic division to divide $f(x)$ by $(x-2):$

$$
\begin{aligned} & {x}^{3} & {x}^{2} & {x}^{1} & {x}^{0} \\ 2 & -1 & 7 & -14 & 8 \\  &  & -2 & 10 & -8 \\  & -1 & 5 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}
$$

We obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x-2)(-{x}^{2}+5x-4) \\  & =-(x-2)({x}^{2}-5x+4) \\  & =-(x-2)(x-1)(x-4).\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the factors equal to zero, we find that the other roots of $f(x)$ are $x=1$ and $x=4.$ 

Now, let's find the $y$-intercept. To do that, we substitute $x=0,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-(0-2)(0-1)(0-4) \\  & =-(-2)(-1)(-4) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we draw an $S$-shaped graph that passes through the three roots $x=1,2,4$ and has the $y$-intercept $y=8,$ as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14250730/assets/21dec37151f40778b8f094d3ae68cd8716c993535e53496cf7f148817c72e345.png)

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
Given that $(x+3)$ is a factor of $f(x)={x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}-9x-18,$ which of the following curves is generated by $y=f(x)?$

(*Note: Figures not drawn to scale*)
questions.worked_solution:
First, we note that the function is a positive cubic curve because the coefficient of ${x}^{3}$ is positive.

We are told that $(x+3)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ so to find the other roots of $f(x)$ we use synthetic division to divide $f(x)$ by  $(x+3):$

$$
\begin{aligned} & {x}^{3} & {x}^{2} & {x}^{1} & {x}^{0} \\ -3 & 1 & 2 & -9 & -18 \\  &  & -3 & 3 & 18 \\  & 1 & -1 & -6 & 0\end{aligned}
$$

We obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x+3)({x}^{2}-x-6) \\  & =(x+3)(x+2)(x-3),\end{aligned}
$$

so the roots of $f(x)$ are $x=-3,$ $x=-2,$ and $x=3.$ 

Now, let's find the $y$-intercept. To do that, we substitute $x=0,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =(0+3)(0+2)(0-3) \\  & =(3)(2)(-3) \\  & =-18.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we draw an inverted $\text{S}$-shaped graph that passes through the three roots $x=-3,-2,3$ and has the $y$-intercept $y=-18,$ as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14250730/assets/c3d41c300747f4f0f18607351f2f03241c9a789ed70fe72e05c5a385b708c4c8.png)

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
Given that $x=2$ is a root of $f(x)=-{x}^{3}+7{x}^{2}-14x+8,$ which of the following curves is generated by $y=f(x)?$

(*Note: Figures not drawn to scale*)
question.worked_solution:
First, we notice that the function is a negative cubic curve because the coefficient of ${x}^{3}$ is negative.

We are told that $x=2$ is a root of $f(x),$ which means that $(x-2)$ is a factor of $f(x).$ So, to find the other roots of $f(x)$ we use synthetic division to divide $f(x)$ by $(x-2):$

$$
\begin{aligned} & {x}^{3} & {x}^{2} & {x}^{1} & {x}^{0} \\ 2 & -1 & 7 & -14 & 8 \\  &  & -2 & 10 & -8 \\  & -1 & 5 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}
$$

We obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x-2)(-{x}^{2}+5x-4) \\  & =-(x-2)({x}^{2}-5x+4) \\  & =-(x-2)(x-1)(x-4).\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the factors equal to zero, we find that the other roots of $f(x)$ are $x=1$ and $x=4.$ 

Now, let's find the $y$-intercept. To do that, we substitute $x=0,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-(0-2)(0-1)(0-4) \\  & =-(-2)(-1)(-4) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we draw an $S$-shaped graph that passes through the three roots $x=1,2,4$ and has the $y$-intercept $y=8,$ as follows:

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Find the minimum value of $y$ on the graph $y=|x+4|-1.$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that $y=|x-h|+k$ is a vertical translation of the absolute value graph $y=|x|$ by $h$ units right and $k$ units up.

The function $y=|x+4|-1$ has $h=-4$ and $k=-1.$ Therefore, it is a translation of the absolute value graph $y=|x|$ by $4$ units *left* and $1$ unit *down*.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14250789/assets/45411bac1f347093b8b9931e1f8f8bee4f1eb411b6256a4c56d0ba33cffe603e.png)

Looking at the graph, we can see that the minimum value of $y$ is $-1.$ This occurs at the point $(-4,-1).$

a
3
b
−13
c
13
d
−3
e
0
Submit
Correct

Remember that y=|x−h|+k is a vertical translation of the absolute value graph y=|x| by h units right and k units up.

The function y=|x−3|+3 has h=3 and k=3. Therefore, it is a translation of the absolute value graph y=|x| by 3 units right and 3 units up.

Looking at the graph, we can see that the minimum value of y is 3. This occurs at the point (3,3).

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Given the statement

$$
P:2\text{ divides }8
$$

 
which of the following represents the statement $¬P?$
questions.worked_solution:
The symbol "$¬$" represents negation. So, our task is to negate the given sentence. 

To negate our plain English sentence, we place the words "It is not true that" in front of it. This gives the following:

$$
¬P:\text{It is not true that }2\text{ divides }8,
$$

 

In other words, $2$ does *not* divide $8.$ Therefore, $¬P$ means the following:

$$
¬P:2\text{ does }\text{not}\text{ divide }8.
$$

Note that $P$ is **true,** while $¬P$ is **false.**

questions.problem:
Given the statement

$$
P:0\text{ is }\text{not}\text{ greater than }0.1
$$

 
which of the following represents $¬P?$
questions.worked_solution:
The symbol "$¬$" represents negation. So, our task is to negate the given sentence. 

To negate our plain English sentence, we place the words "It is not true that" in front of it. This gives the following:

$$
¬P:\text{It is }\text{not}\text{ true that }0\text{ is }\text{not}\text{ greater than }0.1,
$$

 

In other words, $0$ is greater than $0.1.$ Therefore, $¬P$ means the following:

$$
¬P:0\text{ is greater than }0.1.
$$

Note that $P$ is **true,** while $¬P$ is **false.**

questions.problem:
Consider the following statement.

$5$ is **not** prime.

What is the negation of this statement?
questions.worked_solution:
Let's denote the given statement as $P.$

The symbol "$¬$" represents negation. So, our task is to negate the given sentence. 

To negate our plain English sentence, we place the words "It is not true that" in front of it. This gives the following:

It is **not** true that $5$ is **not** prime.

In other words, $5$ is prime. Therefore, $¬P$ means the following:

$5$ is prime.

Note that $P$ is **false,** while $¬P$ is **true.**

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
Consider the following statement.

$5$ belongs to the set of integer numbers.

What is the negation of this statement?
questions.worked_solution:
Let's denote the given statement as $P.$

The symbol "$¬$" represents negation. So, our task is to negate the given sentence. 

To negate our plain English sentence, we place the words "It is not true that" in front of it. This gives the following:

It is not true that $5$  belongs to the set of integer numbers.

In other words, $5$ does *not* belong to the set of integer numbers. Therefore, $¬P$ means the following:

$5$ does **not** belong to the set of integer numbers.

Note that $P$ is **true,** while $¬P$ is **false.**

questions.problem:
$10$ is **not** a prime number, and $0.1$ is a real number.

The sentence

$10$ is **not** a prime number 

can be expressed symbolically as $¬P.$

$0.1$ is a real number 

can be expressed symbolically as $Q.$

Therefore, the sentence

$10$ is **not** a prime number, and $0.1$ is a real number

can be expressed symbolically as $¬P∧Q.$

can be expressed symbolically as $¬P∨Q.$

questions.problem:
Find the missing values in the following truth table:

| $\,P\,$ | $\,Q\,$ | $\,P∨¬Q\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | {{field-1}} |

| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | {{field-4}} |
questions.worked_solution:
First, we add a column for $¬Q,$ where the truth values are opposite to the corresponding values in the column for $Q.$ 

| $\,P\,$ | $\,Q\,$ | $\,¬Q\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |

Then, we add a column for $P∨¬Q.$ Remember that $P∨¬Q$ is true if either $P$ is true or $¬Q$ is true. 

| $\,P\,$ | $\,Q\,$ | $\,¬Q\,$ | $\,P∨¬Q\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |

questions.name: Question 12
questions.problem:
Find the missing values in the following truth table:

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,¬(¬A∨B)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | {{field-1}} |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | {{field-2}} |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | {{field-3}} |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | {{field-4}} |
questions.worked_solution:
First, we add a column for $¬A,$ where the truth values are opposite to the corresponding values in the column for $A.$ 

| $\,A\,$ | $\,¬A\,$ | $\,B\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |

Then, we add a column for $¬A∨B.$ Remember that $¬A∨B$ is true if either $¬A$ is true or $B$ is true. 

| $\,A\,$ | $\,¬A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,¬A∨B\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |

Finally, we add a column for $¬(¬A∨B),$ where the truth values are opposite to the corresponding values in the column for $¬A∨B.$ 

| $\,A\,$ | $\,¬A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,¬A∨B\,$ | $\,¬(¬A∨B)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |

questions.name: Question 13
questions.problem:
Find the missing values in the following truth table:

| $\,P\,$ | $\,Q\,$ | $\,¬(P∨¬Q)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | {{field-1}} |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | {{field-2}} |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | {{field-3}} |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | {{field-4}} |
questions.worked_solution:
First, we add a column for $¬Q,$ where the truth values are opposite to the corresponding values in the column for $Q.$ 

| $\,P\,$ | $\,Q\,$ | $\,¬Q\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |

Then, we add a column for $P∨¬Q.$ Remember that $P∨¬Q$ is true if either $P$ is true or $¬Q$ is true. 

| $\,P\,$ | $\,Q\,$ | $\,¬Q\,$ | $\,P∨¬Q\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |

Finally, we add a column for $¬(P∨¬Q),$ where the truth values are opposite to the corresponding values in the column $P∧¬Q.$

| $\,P\,$ | $\,Q\,$ | $\,¬Q\,$ | $\,P∨¬Q\,$ | $\,¬(P∨¬Q)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |

questions.name: Question 14
questions.problem:
Find the missing values in the following truth table:

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,¬(A∧B)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | {{field-1}} |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | {{field-2}} |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | {{field-3}} |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | {{field-4}} |
questions.worked_solution:
First, we add a column for $A∧B.$ Remember that $A∧B$ is true if both $A$ and $B$ are true.

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,A∧B\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |

Then, we add a column for $¬(A∧B).$ Remember that the truth values of $¬(A∧B)$ are opposite those of $A∧B.$

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,A∧B\,$ | $\,¬(A∧B)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |

questions.name: Question 16
questions.problem: Simplify the statement $¬(¬P)∨¬(¬(P∧Q)).$
questions.worked_solution:
Two negations in a row cancel each other out. So: 

- we can simplify $¬(¬P)$ to $P,$ and

- we can also simplify $¬(¬(P∧Q))$ to $P∧Q.$

Therefore, the given statement can be simplified to 

$$
P∨(P∧Q).
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Negating a Plain English Statement
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the following statement.

$P: 1$ is **not** smaller than $2$

What statement represents $\neg P?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The symbol "$\neg$" represents negation. So, our task is to negate the given sentence. 

To negate our plain English sentence, we place the words "It is not true that" in front of it. This gives the following:

It is **not** true that $1$ is **not** smaller than $2.$

In other words, $1$ is smaller than $2.$ Therefore, $\neg P$ means the following:

$1$ is smaller than $2.$

Note that $P$ is **false,** while $\neg P$ is **true.**

Example: 
                    Expressing a Negated Sentence in Symbolic Form
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the following statement:

$\dfrac12$ is **not** a natural number, or $\sqrt{2}$ is **not** a real number.

Express the compound statement above in symbolic form given the following:

- ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14250694/assets/93d591c3e613da2fe970a5082d8528031a23a3dbd57006cacdc529105fe2d348.svg)

- ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14250694/assets/ca9dfdb43a7191b43b65eedce9ef0fed92465bcafdfdad6c813ed4c6c01257de.svg)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The sentence

 $\dfrac12$ is **not** a natural number 

can be expressed symbolically as $\neg P.$ 

The sentence

$\sqrt{2}$ is **not** a real number 

can be expressed symbolically as $\neg Q.$

Therefore, the sentence

 $\dfrac12$ is **not** a natural number, or $\sqrt{2}$ is **not** a real number

can be expressed symbolically as $\neg P \lor \neg Q.$

canonical_examples.problem:
Find the missing values in the following truth table:

| $\,P\,$ | $\,Q\,$ | $\, \neg (P \land \neg Q)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\phantom{F}}$ |

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Simplifying a Double Negation
canonical_examples.problem:
Simplify the statement $
eg(
eg C) \lor 
eg(
eg(C \land D)).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Two negations in a row cancel each other out. So: 

- we can simplify $\neg(\neg C)$ to $C,$ and

- we can also simplify $\neg(\neg(C \land D))$ to $C \land D.$

Therefore, the given statement can be simplified to 

$$
C \lor (C \land D).
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
The **negation** of a mathematical statement is its *opposite* statement. A mathematical statement and its negation have opposite truth values. 

For example: 

- The negation of the *true* statement "$4$ is divisible by $2$" is the *false* statement "$4$ is **not** divisible by $2.$"

- The negation of the *false* statement "$5$ is even" is the *true* statement "$5$ is odd."

We can express negations using the symbol "$\neg$". The negation of $A$ is denoted $\neg A,$ and has the opposite truth values as $A{:}$

| $\,A\,$ | $\,\neg A\,$ |
| --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |

We can negate compound statements as well. For example, the statement $\neg (A \land B)$ has the opposite truth values as the statement $A \land B{:}$

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\, A \land B \,$ | $\, \neg (A \land B) \,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |

tutorials.name: Double Negations
tutorials.problem:
When we have two negations in a row, we can cancel them out.

- For example, $\neg (\neg A)$ can be simplified to $A.$

- Likewise, $\neg (\neg (A \land B))$ can be simplified to $A \land B.$

To understand why negations cancel with each other, consider the following statement: 

$4$ is divisible by $2.$

The negation of this statement is 

$4$ is **not** divisible by $2.$

If we negate again, we get back the original sentence: 

$4$ divisible by $2.$

So, if we negate a statement twice, we end up with the original statement.

More formally, we can prove that $\neg (\neg A) \equiv A$ using a truth table.

| $\,A\,$ | $\,\neg A\,$ | $\,\neg(\neg A)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ |

Since $A$ and $\neg(\neg A)$ have the same truth values, they are logically equivalent.

- The negation of the *true* statement "$4$ is divisible by $2$" is the *false* statement "$4$ is **not** divisible by $2.$"

- The negation of the *false* statement "$5$ is even" is the *true* statement "$5$ is odd."

We can express negations using the symbol "$\neg$". The negation of $A$ is denoted $\neg A,$ and has the opposite truth values as $A{:}$

| $\,A\,$ | $\,\neg A\,$ |
| --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |

We can negate compound statements as well. For example, the statement $\neg (A \land B)$ has the opposite truth values as the statement $A \land B{:}$

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\, A \land B \,$ | $\, \neg (A \land B) \,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |

2 divides 8.

tutorial.name: Double Negations
tutorial.problem:
When we have two negations in a row, we can cancel them out.

- For example, $\neg (\neg A)$ can be simplified to $A.$

- Likewise, $\neg (\neg (A \land B))$ can be simplified to $A \land B.$

To understand why negations cancel with each other, consider the following statement: 

$4$ is divisible by $2.$

The negation of this statement is 

$4$ is **not** divisible by $2.$

If we negate again, we get back the original sentence: 

$4$ divisible by $2.$

So, if we negate a statement twice, we end up with the original statement.

More formally, we can prove that $\neg (\neg A) \equiv A$ using a truth table.

| $\,A\,$ | $\,\neg A\,$ | $\,\neg(\neg A)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ |

Since $A$ and $\neg(\neg A)$ have the same truth values, they are logically equivalent.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Two negations in a row cancel each other out. So: 

- we can simplify $\neg(\neg C)$ to $C,$ and

- we can also simplify $\neg(\neg(C \land D))$ to $C \land D.$

Therefore, the given statement can be simplified to 

$$
C \lor (C \land D).
$$

question.html:
Question 16
?

Simplify the statement ¬(¬P)∨¬(¬(P∧Q)).

a
P∨(P∧¬Q)
b
¬P∨(P∧Q)
c
P∨(P∧Q)
d
P∨¬(P∧Q)
e
¬P∨(¬P∧Q)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Two negations in a row cancel each other out. So:

  • we can simplify ¬(¬P) to P, and

  • we can also simplify ¬(¬(P∧Q)) to P∧Q.

Therefore, the given statement can be simplified to

P∨(P∧Q).

question.html:
Question 19
?

Simplify the statement ¬[¬(A∧¬(¬B))]∨B.

a
(A∧B)∨B
b
(¬A∧¬B)∨B
c
(¬A∧B)∨B
d
(A∧¬B)∨B
e
¬(A∧B)∨B
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Two negations in a row cancel each other out. So, we can simplify ¬(¬B) to B.

As a result of this, the statement simplifes to

¬(¬(A∧B))∨B.

Then, we can simplify ¬(¬(A∧B)) to A∧B.

Therefore, the given statement can be simplified to

(A∧B)∨B.

Introduction

The negation of a mathematical statement is its opposite statement. A mathematical statement and its negation have opposite truth values.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Given the statement

$$
P:2\text{ divides }8
$$

 
which of the following represents the statement $¬P?$
question.worked_solution:
The symbol "$¬$" represents negation. So, our task is to negate the given sentence. 

To negate our plain English sentence, we place the words "It is not true that" in front of it. This gives the following:

$$
¬P:\text{It is not true that }2\text{ divides }8,
$$

 

In other words, $2$ does *not* divide $8.$ Therefore, $¬P$ means the following:

$$
¬P:2\text{ does }\text{not}\text{ divide }8.
$$

Note that $P$ is **true,** while $¬P$ is **false.**

question.html:
Question 1
?

Given the statement P:2 divides 8 which of the following represents the statement ¬P?

a
8 does not divide 2.
b
not 2 divides 8.
c
2 divides 8.
d
8 divides 2.
e
2 does not divide 8.
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The symbol "¬" represents negation. So, our task is to negate the given sentence.

To negate our plain English sentence, we place the words "It is not true that" in front of it. This gives the following:

¬P:It is not true that 2 divides 8,

In other words, 2 does not divide 8. Therefore, ¬P means the following:

¬P:2 does not divide 8.

Note that P is true, while ¬P is false.
question.knowledge_point: Negating a Plain English Statement

feedback.html:
Question 1
?

Given the statement P:2 divides 8 which of the following represents the statement ¬P?

a
8 does not divide 2.
b
not 2 divides 8.
c
2 divides 8.
d
8 divides 2.
e
2 does not divide 8.
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The symbol "¬" represents negation. So, our task is to negate the given sentence.

To negate our plain English sentence, we place the words "It is not true that" in front of it. This gives the following:

¬P:It is not true that 2 divides 8,

In other words, 2 does not divide 8. Therefore, ¬P means the following:

¬P:2 does not divide 8.

Note that P is true, while ¬P is false.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
Given the statement

$$
P:0\text{ is }\text{not}\text{ greater than }0.1
$$

 
which of the following represents $¬P?$
question.worked_solution:
The symbol "$¬$" represents negation. So, our task is to negate the given sentence. 

To negate our plain English sentence, we place the words "It is not true that" in front of it. This gives the following:

$$
¬P:\text{It is }\text{not}\text{ true that }0\text{ is }\text{not}\text{ greater than }0.1,
$$

 

In other words, $0$ is greater than $0.1.$ Therefore, $¬P$ means the following:

$$
¬P:0\text{ is greater than }0.1.
$$

Note that $P$ is **true,** while $¬P$ is **false.**

question.html:
Question 2
?

Given the statement P:0 is not greater than 0.1 which of the following represents ¬P?

a
0.1 is not greater than 0.
b
0.1 is greater than 0.
c
0 is equal to 0.1.
d
0 is greater than 0.1.
e
0 is not greater than 0.1.
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The symbol "¬" represents negation. So, our task is to negate the given sentence.

To negate our plain English sentence, we place the words "It is not true that" in front of it. This gives the following:

¬P:It is not true that 0 is not greater than 0.1,

In other words, 0 is greater than 0.1. Therefore, ¬P means the following:

¬P:0 is greater than 0.1.

Note that P is true, while ¬P is false.

question.html:
Question 2
?

Given the statement P:0 is not greater than 0.1 which of the following represents ¬P?

a
0.1 is not greater than 0.
b
0.1 is greater than 0.
c
0 is equal to 0.1.
d
0 is greater than 0.1.
e
0 is not greater than 0.1.
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The symbol "¬" represents negation. So, our task is to negate the given sentence.

To negate our plain English sentence, we place the words "It is not true that" in front of it. This gives the following:

¬P:It is not true that 0 is not greater than 0.1,

In other words, 0 is greater than 0.1. Therefore, ¬P means the following:

¬P:0 is greater than 0.1.

Note that P is true, while ¬P is false.
question.knowledge_point: Negating a Plain English Statement

solution.reasoning: Negating “0 is not greater than 0.1” cancels the negation, giving “0 is greater than 0.1,” option d. P is true and its negation is false. No captured MA answer or grade establishes this question’s key.

question.html:
Question 5
?

Consider the following statement.

0.75 does not belong to the set of rational numbers.

What is the negation of this statement?

a
0.75 belongs to the set of rational numbers.
b
0.75 does not belong to the set of rational numbers.
c
0.75 does not belong to the set of integer numbers.
d
0.75 belongs to the set of integer numbers.
e
0.75 belongs to the set of real numbers.
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's denote the given statement as P.

The symbol "¬" represents negation. So, our task is to negate the given sentence.

To negate our plain English sentence, we place the words "It is not true that" in front of it. This gives the following:

It is not true that 0.75 does not belong to the set of rational numbers.

In other words, 0.75 belongs to the set of rational numbers. Therefore, ¬P means the following:

0.75 belongs to the set of rational numbers.

Note that P is false, while ¬P is true.

question.name: Question 6
question.problem:
$10$ is **not** a prime number, and $0.1$ is a real number.

Express the compound statement above in symbolic form given the following:

- $P:10\text{ is a prime number}$

- $Q:0.1\text{ is a real number}$
question.worked_solution:
The negation is represented by the symbol "$¬$".

The sentence

$10$ is **not** a prime number 

can be expressed symbolically as $¬P.$ 

The sentence

$0.1$ is a real number 

can be expressed symbolically as $Q.$

Therefore, the sentence

$10$ is **not** a prime number, and $0.1$ is a real number

can be expressed symbolically as $¬P∧Q.$

question.name: Question 12
question.problem:
Find the missing values in the following truth table:

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,¬(¬A∨B)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | {{field-1}} |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | {{field-2}} |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | {{field-3}} |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | {{field-4}} |
question.worked_solution:
First, we add a column for $¬A,$ where the truth values are opposite to the corresponding values in the column for $A.$ 

| $\,A\,$ | $\,¬A\,$ | $\,B\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |

Then, we add a column for $¬A∨B.$ Remember that $¬A∨B$ is true if either $¬A$ is true or $B$ is true. 

| $\,A\,$ | $\,¬A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,¬A∨B\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |

Finally, we add a column for $¬(¬A∨B),$ where the truth values are opposite to the corresponding values in the column for $¬A∨B.$ 

| $\,A\,$ | $\,¬A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,¬A∨B\,$ | $\,¬(¬A∨B)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |

Find the missing values in the following truth table:
P Q ¬(P∨¬Q)
T T
F

F
T F
F
F
T
F T
T
T
F
F F
F
F
T
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we add a column for ¬Q, where the truth values are opposite to the corresponding values in the column for Q.

P Q ¬Q
T T F
T F T
F T F
F F T

Then, we add a column for P∨¬Q. Remember that P∨¬Q is true if either P is true or ¬Q is true.

P Q ¬Q P∨¬Q
T T F T
T F T T
F T F F

Finally, we add a column for ¬(P∨¬Q), where the truth values are opposite to the corresponding values in the column P∧¬Q.

P Q ¬Q P∨¬Q ¬(P∨¬Q)
T T F T F
T F T T F
F T F F T
F F T T F

solution.reasoning: By De Morgan’s law, ¬(P∨¬Q) equals ¬P∧Q, which is true only when P is false and Q is true. The rows are F, F, T, F. No captured MA answer or grade establishes this question’s key.

question.problem:
Find the missing values in the following truth table:

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,¬(A∧B)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | {{field-1}} |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | {{field-2}} |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | {{field-3}} |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | {{field-4}} |
question.worked_solution:
First, we add a column for $A∧B.$ Remember that $A∧B$ is true if both $A$ and $B$ are true.

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,A∧B\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |

Then, we add a column for $¬(A∧B).$ Remember that the truth values of $¬(A∧B)$ are opposite those of $A∧B.$

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,A∧B\,$ | $\,¬(A∧B)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |

Question 14
?
Find the missing values in the following truth table:
A B ¬(A∧B)
T T
T
T
F
T F
T
T
F
F T
T
F
T
F F
T
F
T
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we add a column for A∧B. Remember that A∧B is true if both A and B are true.

A B A∧B
T T T
T F F
F T F
F F F

Then, we add a column for ¬(A∧B). Remember that the truth values of ¬(A∧B) are opposite those of A∧B.

A B A∧B ¬(A∧B)
T T T F
T F F T
F T F T
F F F T

question.name: Question 16
question.problem: Simplify the statement $¬(¬P)∨¬(¬(P∧Q)).$
question.worked_solution:
Two negations in a row cancel each other out. So: 

- we can simplify $¬(¬P)$ to $P,$ and

- we can also simplify $¬(¬(P∧Q))$ to $P∧Q.$

Therefore, the given statement can be simplified to 

$$
P∨(P∧Q).
$$

question.html:
Question 16
?

Simplify the statement ¬(¬P)∨¬(¬(P∧Q)).

a
P∨(P∧¬Q)
b
¬P∨(P∧Q)
c
P∨(P∧Q)
d
P∨¬(P∧Q)
e
¬P∨(¬P∧Q)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Two negations in a row cancel each other out. So:

  • we can simplify ¬(¬P) to P, and

  • we can also simplify ¬(¬(P∧Q)) to P∧Q.

Therefore, the given statement can be simplified to

P∨(P∧Q).

question.html:
Question 16
?

Simplify the statement ¬(¬P)∨¬(¬(P∧Q)).

a
P∨(P∧¬Q)
b
¬P∨(P∧Q)
c
P∨(P∧Q)
d
P∨¬(P∧Q)
e
¬P∨(¬P∧Q)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Two negations in a row cancel each other out. So:

  • we can simplify ¬(¬P) to P, and

  • we can also simplify ¬(¬(P∧Q)) to P∧Q.

Therefore, the given statement can be simplified to

P∨(P∧Q).

question.html:
Question 17
?

Simplify the statement ¬[¬(¬B∨¬(¬A))].

a
¬(¬B∨A)
b
¬B∨A
c
¬B∨¬A
d
B∨A
e
B∨¬A
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Two negations in a row cancel each other out. So, we can simplify ¬(¬A) to A.

As a result of this, the statement simplifes to

¬[¬(¬B∨A)]

Then, we can simplify ¬(¬(¬B∨A)) to ¬B∨A.

Therefore, the given statement can be simplified to

¬B∨A.

solution.reasoning: The two outer negations cancel, leaving ¬B∨¬(¬A). The double negation of A also cancels, giving ¬B∨A, option b. No captured MA answer or grade establishes this question’s key.

question.name: Question 19
question.problem: Simplify the statement $¬[¬(A∧¬(¬B))]∨B.$
question.worked_solution:
Two negations in a row cancel each other out. So, we can simplify $¬(¬B)$ to $B.$ 

As a result of this, the statement simplifes to 

$$
¬(¬(A∧B))∨B.
$$

Then, we can simplify $¬(¬(A∧B))$ to $A∧B.$

Therefore, the given statement can be simplified to 

$$
(A∧B)∨B.
$$

question.html:
Question 19
?

Simplify the statement ¬[¬(A∧¬(¬B))]∨B.

a
(A∧B)∨B
b
(¬A∧¬B)∨B
c
(¬A∧B)∨B
d
(A∧¬B)∨B
e
¬(A∧B)∨B
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Two negations in a row cancel each other out. So, we can simplify ¬(¬B) to B.

As a result of this, the statement simplifes to

¬(¬(A∧B))∨B.

Then, we can simplify ¬(¬(A∧B)) to A∧B.

Therefore, the given statement can be simplified to

(A∧B)∨B.

(A∧B)∨B.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Suppose $X$ is a $5\times 5$ matrix and $det(X)=55.$ The matrix $Y$ is obtained from $X$ by applying the elementary row operation ${R}_{5}↔{R}_{3}$ (switching the fifth and the third rows). What is the value of $det(Y)?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since swapping any two rows changes the sign of the determinant to the opposite sign, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(Y) & =-det(X) \\  & =-(55) \\  & =-55.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 11
questions.problem: Suppose $C$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $det(C)=-5.$ What is the value of $det(-4C)?$
questions.worked_solution:
Multiplying a $n\times n$ matrix by a scalar $k$ is equivalent to multiplying each row by $k,$ and this occurs $n$ times. This leads to the result

$$
\begin{aligned}det(k\cdot C)={k}^{n}\cdot det(C).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have $k=-4$ and $n=3.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}det(-4C) & =(-4)^{3}\cdot det(C) \\  & =(-64)\cdot (-5) \\  & =320.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Suppose $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $det(A)=4.$ What is the value of $det(5A)?$
questions.worked_solution:
Multiplying a $n\times n$ matrix by a scalar $k$ is equivalent to multiplying each row by $k,$ and this occurs $n$ times. This leads to the result

$$
\begin{aligned}det(k\cdot A)={k}^{n}\cdot det(A).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have $k=5$ and $n=3.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}det(5A) & ={5}^{3}\cdot det(A) \\  & =125\cdot 4 \\  & =500.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 16
questions.problem: Suppose $U$ is a $4\times 4$ matrix and $det(U)=21.$ The matrix $V$ is obtained from $U$ by applying the elementary row operations ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-7){R}_{4}$ and ${R}_{3}:=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{3}.$ What is the value of $det(V)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's figure out what each operation does to the determinant.

- The operation ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-7){R}_{4}$ involves adding a multiple of one row to another row,  so it does not change the determinant.

- The operation ${R}_{3}:=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{3}$ involves multiplying a row by $\frac{1}{3},$ so the determinant is multiplied by $\frac{1}{3}$ as well.

Therefore, we only have to multiply the determinant by $\frac{1}{3}.$ Consequently, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}det(V) & =\frac{1}{3}det(U) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot 21 \\  & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 17
questions.problem: Suppose $B$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $det(B)=-7.$ The matrix $C$ is obtained from $B$ by applying the elementary row operations ${R}_{2}:=2{R}_{2}$ and ${R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}.$ What is the value of $det(C)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's figure out what each operation does to the determinant.

- The operation ${R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}$ involves swapping two rows, so it changes the sign of the determinant to the opposite one.

- The operation ${R}_{2}:=2{R}_{2}$ involves multiplying a row by $2,$ so the determinant is multiplied by $2$ as well.

Therefore, we have to change the sign of the determinant to the opposite one and multiply by $2$ as well. Consequently, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}det(C) & =2\cdot (-det(B)) \\  & =-2det(B) \\  & =-2\cdot (-7) \\  & =14.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 19
questions.problem: Suppose $A$ is a $5\times 5$ matrix and $det(A)=6.$ The matrix $B$ is obtained from $A$ by applying the elementary row operations ${R}_{2}↔{R}_{3}$ and ${R}_{3}:=4{R}_{3}.$ What is the value of $det(B)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's figure out what each operation does to the determinant.

- The operation ${R}_{2}↔{R}_{3}$ involves swapping two rows, so it changes the sign of the determinant to the opposite one.

- The operation ${R}_{3}:=4{R}_{3}$ involves multiplying a row by $4,$ so the determinant is multiplied by $4$ as well.

Therefore, we have to change the sign of the determinant to the opposite one and multiply by $4$ as well. Consequently, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}det(B) & =4\cdot (-det(A)) \\  & =-4det(A) \\  & =-4\cdot 6 \\  & =-24.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 20
questions.problem: Suppose $A$ is a $4\times 4$ matrix and $det(A)=11.$ The matrix $B$ is obtained from $A$ by applying the elementary row operations ${R}_{4}:=3{R}_{4}$ and ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-5){R}_{1}.$ What is the value of $det(B)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's figure out what each operation does to the determinant.

- The operation ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-5){R}_{1}$ involves adding a multiple of one row to another row,  so it does not change the determinant.

- The operation ${R}_{4}:=3{R}_{4}$ involves multiplying a row by $3,$ so the determinant is multiplied by $3$ as well.

Therefore, we only have to multiply the determinant by $3.$ Consequently, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}det(B) & =3det(A) \\  & =3\cdot 11 \\  & =33.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 21
questions.problem:
Given that $det(A)=det(B),$ which of the following elementary row operations transforms matrix $A$ to matrix $B,$ where

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 & -2 \\ 2 & 8 & -2\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & -8\end{aligned}]?
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $det(A)=det(B)$, the row operation applied to $A$ must be to add or subtract a multiple of one row to another row. In other words, it is of the form 

$$
{R}_{j}:={R}_{j}+(k){R}_{i},\,i\ne j.
$$

By considering the given row operations that are of the above form, we notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 5 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 & -2 \\ 2 & 8 & -2\end{aligned}| & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 5 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & -8\end{aligned}| \\  & =det(B).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the required row operation is

$$
{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1}.
$$

questions.name: Question 23
questions.problem:
Given that $det(A)=det(B),$ which of the following elementary row operations transforms matrix $A$ to matrix $B,$ where

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 4 & -1 \\ 3 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & -9 \\ 3 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]?
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $det(A)=det(B)$, the row operation applied to $A$ must be to add or subtract a multiple of one row to another row. In other words, it is of the form 

$$
{R}_{j}:={R}_{j}+(k){R}_{i},\,i\ne j.
$$

By considering the given row operations that are of the above form, we notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 4 & -1 \\ 3 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}| & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & -9 \\ 3 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =det(B).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the required row operation is

$$
{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1}.
$$

questions.name: Question 24
questions.problem:
Consider the matrices given below. Given that $A$ and $B$ are row equivalent matrices and $det(A)=-108$, find $det(B).$

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 & -1 \\ -2 & -4 & 2 \\ 3 & 6 & 3\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 3 & 6 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that $B$ can be obtained from $A$ by multiplying the $2$nd row by $-\frac{1}{2}.$ 

So, the determinant is multiplied by $-\frac{1}{2}$ as well.
Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}det(B) & =-\frac{1}{2}\cdot det(A) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-108) \\  & =54.\end{aligned}
$$
